docs.title: pipekit
docs.text:
Composable scientific pipelines. Train, register, deploy — one operator interface end-to-end.

pipekit is a uv workspace of seven Python packages that together turn the pieces of a scientific ML workflow into composable Operators: data loading, QC, training, data assimilation, model registry, reproducibility. The same operator that returns a trained emulator drops into a forecast Cycle as a step function. One mental model, one composition surface, end to end.

from pipekit_cycle import Cycle, NeuralForward
from pipekit_experiment import LocalModelRegistry

# Reload a trained model by name and forecast 24 steps with it
# as the forward model — same Operator interface as inference.
registry = LocalModelRegistry("/models")
op = registry.load("methane_emulator_v3")

forecast = Cycle(step_op=NeuralForward(op, dt=3600.0), n_steps=24)
final_state, _ = forecast(x0, None)

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: A 10-minute mental model of what pipekit is and how the pieces fit together. If you've used scikit-learn pipelines or Keras's functional API the shapes will look familiar — pipekit is the same idea generalised to arbitrary data carriers (arrays, xr.Dataset, GeoTensor, custom dataclasses) and extended to data assimilation, training, and reproducibility.

docs.title: The one-paragraph version
docs.text: You write a small Operator class for each piece of work (load, mask, diff, train, infer, …). pipekit gives you the glue: composition with |, branching / retry / quarantine, structured observation, parallel mapping, caching, YAML round-trip with content hashing, and a state substrate for time-stepping. Sister packages add domain pieces on top (pipekit-cycle for data assimilation, pipekit-train for training, pipekit-array for Array-API-dispatched numerical operators, pipekit-experiment for the registry / tracker boundary).

docs.title: 1. Operators
docs.text:
An Operator is a class with one method: _apply(self, carrier) -> carrier. The carrier can be anything — a numpy array, an xarray Dataset, a GeoTensor, a pandas DataFrame, a dataclass, even an iterable of carriers. The carrier flows through; each operator does its work and returns the next carrier.

from pipekit import Operator


class Scale(Operator):
    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        self.factor = factor

    def _apply(self, x):
        return x * self.factor


Scale(2.0)(5.0)  # → 10.0

The base class handles __call__, configuration round-trip (via get_config()), graph node construction (when used inside Graph), and content hashing. You only implement _apply.

docs.title: 2. Composition with |
docs.text:
The pipe operator chains operators into a Sequential:

from pipekit import Sequential, Tap


pipe = Scale(2.0) | Tap(print, name="log") | Scale(3.0)
pipe(5.0)  # → 30.0; the Tap prints "10.0" between scales

Sequential is itself an Operator, so you can compose pipelines into bigger pipelines.

For non-linear flows — multiple inputs, fan-in, fan-out — use Graph with named nodes:

from pipekit import Graph, Input


g = Graph()
a = g.add(Input("a"))
b = g.add(Input("b"))
total = g.add(MyAdder(), inputs=[a, b])
g.set_outputs([total])
g({"a": 3.0, "b": 4.0})  # → {<total.id>: 7.0}

docs.title: 3. Carrier-agnostic by design
docs.text:
The framework doesn't know what a "carrier" is. The base Operator class makes no assumptions about shape, dtype, units, or coordinate system. That's why the same Operator, Sequential, Graph plumbing works across:

graph LR
    PK[pipekit core] -.carrier-agnostic.-> A[numpy array]
    PK -.-> B[xarray Dataset]
    PK -.-> C[GeoTensor]
    PK -.-> D[Custom dataclass]
    PK -.-> E[Iterable of carriers]
    style PK fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff

Sister packages specialise. pipekit-array operators consume any Array API conformant array; pipekit-cycle operators consume (carrier, state) pairs; domain libraries (geotoolz, xr_toolz) ship operators that consume their specific carrier types.

docs.title: 4. State carry — StatefulOperator
docs.text:
Most operators are stateless: they consume a carrier and emit a carrier. But some need to track state across calls — a time-stepping forecast, a training loop, an online statistic. For those, pipekit core ships StatefulOperator and a generic CarryState mechanism:

graph LR
    in_c[carrier in] --> op[StatefulOperator]
    in_s[state in] --> op
    op --> out_c[carrier out]
    op --> out_s[state out]
    out_s -.feeds next step.-> op
    style op fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff

This is the substrate for:

  • pipekit-cycle.Cycle — N steps of (carrier, state) → (carrier, state)
  • pipekit-train.TrainingLoop — the optimizer state, step count, metrics flow as CarryState across batches
  • pipekit-cycle.DACycle — combines a forecast cycle with an observation operator and an analysis step

docs.title: 5. Backend dispatch — pipekit-array
docs.text:
For numerical work, the same operator should run on numpy, JAX, PyTorch, CuPy, or dask. pipekit-array operators dispatch on the Python Array API standard:

from pipekit_array import MeanScalar


# Same operator, different backends — picked at call time:
MeanScalar()(numpy_array)    # uses numpy
MeanScalar()(jax_array)      # uses jax.numpy
MeanScalar()(torch_tensor)   # uses array_api_compat.torch

The mechanism is array_namespace(x) — it returns the module-like namespace shared by all input arrays. Operators close over xp = array_namespace(x) and use xp.mean, xp.concat, xp.stack, etc. for the actual math.

docs.title: Shape inference (where relevant)
docs.text:
Operators that reshape or reduce can opt into static shape inference via compute_output_signature(input_sig) -> Signature | None:

from pipekit.signature import Signature


sig = Signature(dims=(("band", 3), ("y", 256), ("x", 256)), dtype="float32")
pipe = MeanScalar(axis=0) | Subsample(stride=2)
out_sig = pipe.compute_output_signature(sig)
# Signature(dims=(("y", 128), ("x", 128)), dtype="float32")

Sequential.summary walks the pipeline and prints a Keras-style table:

Step                   Output Signature           Params
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
MeanScalar(axis=0)     (y=256, x=256) float32         0
Subsample(stride=2)    (y=128, x=128) float32         0

Operators that don't track shape (raw numpy, GeoTensor) return None from compute_output_signature; the summary prints ? for those steps rather than crashing.

docs.title: YAML round-trip and content hashing
docs.text:
Every operator implements get_config() -> dict[str, Any] (often auto-derived from __init__ parameter names). The framework uses this for:

  • Serialisation — pipekit.dumps(op) → pipekit.loads(json_text) rebuilds a whole pipeline, nested operators and Graphs included; pipekit-experiment's HydraConfigLoader.to_yaml / from_yaml do the same through _target_ YAML. For pipelines you did not write, loads_sandboxed and from_yaml_sandboxed build only registered classes.
  • Content hashing — pipekit.pipeline_hash(op) is a stable hash of the whole configuration. Same pipeline + same config = same hash, deterministically. It is the identifier pipekit-experiment's ModelRegistry stores models under.

Operators that carry user closures (Lambda, Tap, custom callbacks) opt out with forbid_in_yaml: ClassVar[bool] = True — they still work, but their config is a debug repr, not a faithful round-trip.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This page documents the label taxonomy, epic model, and issue conventions used in this project.

docs.title: Label Taxonomy
docs.text:
Every issue carries exactly one type:*, one or more area:*, at most one layer:*, one wave:*, and one priority:*.

Scope Labels Type type:epic-wave, type:epic-theme, type:feature, type:design, type:chore, type:docs, type:bug, type:research Area area:engineering, area:testing, area:docs, area:code — extend per project (e.g. area:algorithmic, area:integration) Layer layer:0-primitives, layer:1-components, layer:2-models — only if the project has a formal layer stack Wave wave:0, wave:1, wave:2, … — release-scoped phases (add wave:N-<slug> variants for descriptive labels) Priority priority:p0 (blocker), priority:p1 (high), priority:p2 (normal)

Bootstrap the standard set on a fresh repo:

make gh-labels

The script lives at .github/scripts/create-labels.sh. Edit the hard-coded create … entries in the script to customise area:*, layer:*, and wave:* for the project, then re-run — the script is idempotent.

docs.title: Two-Layer Epic Model
docs.text:
Work is organised as Wave → Theme → Issue:

[EPIC] Wave N   (L1)   —   release-scoped mega-epic, owns a milestone
  ├── [EPIC] <theme>   (L2)   —   parallel-safe group of issues
  │     ├── feature / design / chore / bug issue
  │     └── …
  └── [EPIC] <theme>   (L2)
        └── …
  • Wave epic (type:epic-wave) maps one-to-one with a milestone (vX.Y-<slug>). Groups several Theme epics that can run in parallel.
  • Theme epic (type:epic-theme) groups concrete issues that ship together as a coherent slice. Themes inside a wave are parallel-safe unless the body says otherwise.
  • Issue (feature / design / chore / bug) is the leaf — a single substantial deliverable that rolls up to a Theme epic.

Stragglers are discouraged: any type:feature issue should attach to a Theme epic. If no suitable theme exists, create one first.

docs.title: Issue Format
docs.text:
Issue templates live in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/:

Template When to use Epic — Wave (L1) Opening a new release-scoped wave Epic — Theme (L2) Grouping related issues inside a wave Feature / Enhancement One substantial deliverable Design / ADR Resolve an open design question for a new API Bug report Something isn't working Research / Comparative Analysis Study prior art (external repo, paper) and produce a prioritized roadmap of follow-up issues

Feature + Design templates include two optional sections for context-heavy issues:

  • Design Snapshot — paste API sketches, code examples, or excerpts from private / external design docs so the issue is self-contained.
  • Mathematical Notes — equations, sign conventions, numerical considerations.

Delete either section if not relevant. Both exist so that an implementer (human or AI agent) can work on the issue without opening other repos or channels.

docs.title: Creating issues
docs.text: New issues should use one of the templates in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ so that labels, required sections, and title conventions are consistent.

docs.title: From the UI
docs.text: Click New issue on the repo's Issues tab and pick a template. The body is pre-filled with the section scaffolding — fill in, apply labels and milestone, submit.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
For drafted content, write the body to a file (minus the template's YAML frontmatter), then:

gh issue create \
  --title "feat(primitives): diagonal BLR update step" \
  --body-file /tmp/issue-body.md \
  --label "type:feature,area:algorithmic,layer:0-primitives,wave:1,priority:p1" \
  --milestone "v0.1-diagonal"

To open the UI in a browser with a template pre-selected:

gh issue create --web

The web flow opens /issues/new/choose so you can pick the template in the UI. gh issue create does not support pre-selecting a template for the web path; the --template flag is only used as starting body text in the non-web flow.

After the issue is created, apply native parent / blocked-by links via the Makefile targets documented below in the Relationships section (or make gh-sub / make gh-block).

docs.title: From Claude Code
docs.text:
The create-gh-issue skill (at .claude/commands/create-gh-issue.md) guides Claude through:

  • Picking the right template (decision tree covering feature / design / bug / research / epic-wave / epic-theme)
  • Drafting the body with required sections + rename guidance for optional sections (Design Snapshot → Demo To Implement, etc.)
  • Applying the correct label set (which type:* + area:* + layer:* + wave:* + priority:* combos are valid for each work type)
  • Setting the milestone (which vX.Y-<slug> corresponds to the wave)
  • Applying relationships (chains to link-gh-issues skill for native sub-issue + blocked-by links)
  • Style conventions — unicode math, text code fences, code-first-prose-last
  • Bulk workflow — publishing a .plans/<wave>-backlog.md file into real GitHub issues (multi-pass: wave epic → theme epics → leaf issues → relationships), with draft-ID → GH-number mapping

Example prompts:

  • "Open a feature issue for the diagonal BLR update step, child of theme epic #27"
  • "File a design issue for the per-parameter prior question"
  • "Publish the drafts in .plans/wave-1-backlog.md as real issues and wire up the sub-issue links"
  • "Open a research issue comparing pof vs this project, based on my notes in <path>"

docs.title: Drafting a wave backlog
docs.text:
For large planning exercises (new wave, new release, large refactor), draft the whole backlog as one markdown file before opening GitHub issues. A template lives at docs/templates/wave-backlog.md.

Why:

  • Review the whole wave in one scroll instead of clicking through 15 half-drafted issues
  • Share context once at the top (Shared Context · Design Snapshot · Intended Package Layout · Runtime Boundary) rather than duplicating across every child issue
  • Stable draft IDs (<PREFIX>-01, <PREFIX>-02, …) let child issues reference each other before GitHub issue numbers exist

Workflow:

  1. Copy docs/templates/wave-backlog.md into your project's .plans/ directory (gitignored). Rename to describe the wave — e.g. .plans/wave-1-backlog.md.
  2. Pick a short project prefix (e.g. PYX for pyrox, OBX for optax_bayes). Number drafts sequentially.
  3. Fill in shared context at the top, then draft each issue body.
  4. When the file is ready, open each draft as a real GitHub issue using the matching .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/. Copy the body verbatim.
  5. Record GitHub issue numbers next to draft IDs in the backlog file, or replace draft IDs throughout. Update cross-references.
  6. Either delete the backlog file or archive it in .plans/archive/.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Use an explicit ## Relationships block at the bottom of each issue / epic body:

## Relationships
- Parent: #<theme-epic>
- Blocked by: #
- Blocks: #
- Related: #

GitHub's task-list feature links bidirectionally from the parent, so checklist items in a Theme epic body auto-show in the referenced issues.

docs.title: Applying native GitHub relationships
docs.text:
The prose ## Relationships block above is a human-readable record. GitHub also exposes two native relationship features that power the UI sub-issue panel and the dependency graph — apply both:

Prose line Native feature Mutation Parent: / Theme Epics / Issues checklist Sub-issues (parent ↔ child hierarchy) addSubIssue / removeSubIssue Blocked by: Typed dependency addBlockedBy Blocks: Inverse — applied on the OTHER issue addBlockedBy (on the blocked side) Related: No native feature prose only

docs.title: From the UI
docs.text:
• Sub-issues — open the parent issue, side-panel → Sub-issues → Create sub-issue or Add existing sub-issue.
  • Blocked by — open the blocked issue, side-panel → Development → Mark as blocked by.

docs.title: From the CLI (Makefile targets)
docs.text:
For scripted work, the repo ships a helper script wrapped by three make targets:

# Link children as sub-issues under a parent
make gh-sub PARENT=7 CHILDREN="42 43 44"

# Mark issue 44 as blocked by 43
make gh-block ISSUE=44 BLOCKED_BY=43

# Inspect parent / sub-issues / blocking / blocked-by for an issue
make gh-show ISSUE=44

Direct script usage (same functionality plus unlink commands):

bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh sub     <parent> <child> [<child> ...]
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh block   <issue> <blocker>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh unsub   <parent> <child>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh unblock <issue> <blocker>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh show    <issue>

The script resolves issue numbers to GraphQL node IDs automatically, and treats "already linked" as a no-op so re-runs are safe.

docs.title: From Claude Code
docs.text:
The link-gh-issues skill (at .claude/commands/link-gh-issues.md) guides Claude through the same operations — useful for bulk-applying relationships from a drafted wave backlog, parsing the Issues checklist out of a theme epic body, or verifying that the native links match the prose.

Example prompts:

  • "Apply the relationships from epic #29"
  • "Link #42, #43, #44 as sub-issues of #7"
  • "Mark #44 as blocked by #43"
  • "What's blocking #44?" (Claude runs make gh-show ISSUE=44 or the underlying GraphQL query)

docs.title: Raw GraphQL (for reference)
docs.text:
Under the hood the helper runs:

mutation { addSubIssue(input: { issueId: "<parent-node-id>", subIssueId: "<child-node-id>" }) { subIssue { number } } }
mutation { addBlockedBy(input: { issueId: "<this-node-id>", blockingIssueId: "<blocker-node-id>" }) { issue { number } } }

Issue node IDs are resolved via gh api repos/:owner/:repo/issues/<N> --jq .node_id.

docs.title: Pre-commit checklist
docs.text:
Run these locally before opening a PR:

make format       # ruff format . + ruff check --fix .   (applies changes)
make lint         # ruff check .                         (CI-style check)
make typecheck    # ty check
make test         # pytest

Note that make format mutates files — it formats and applies autofixes. make lint is the CI-parity read-only check. Run make format first, commit the result, then run make lint / make test to verify.

Pre-commit hooks run ruff on every commit. Run make precommit to apply them to all files manually.

Commit messages follow the Conventional Commits specification — enforced on PR titles by .github/workflows/conventional-commits.yml.

docs.title: A tour of the core
docs.text:
Everything in pipekit, group by group: what it is, when to reach for it, and what it does today.

The core is pure Python with no dependencies. Its public surface is about fifty names in thirteen modules, one module per job, so you can learn it a group at a time. For why it is shaped this way (operators as classes, the carrier left open), read the background; for the shapes real pipelines take, read Patterns.

Every output on this page is from a real run of pipekit 0.0.2.

docs.title: The map
Operator
docs.text:
The class every step subclasses. You write two things: a constructor that stores its arguments under the same names, and _apply. The base class supplies the rest:

  • configuration: get_config() is derived from the constructor's signature (ConfigMixin), and state is a JSON-safe record of the class and its config;
  • rebuilding: Operator.from_state(state) finds the class among every imported subclass and calls it with the config;
  • the pipe: a | b is a Sequential, flattened;
  • two modes in one __call__: on data it runs _apply; on a graph placeholder (Input or Node) it records a node instead;
  • class flags: forbid_in_yaml (holds a closure, so its config cannot be rebuilt) and _terminal (may only end a Sequential);
  • backends: the array backends the operator runs on, such as ("numpy",) or ("numpy", "jax"). Left at None, nothing is checked. When set, an eager call whose carriers or arrays sit on another backend, or on several, raises BackendError before _apply runs, so inputs never move between backends silently.
import pipekit as pk

Scale(2.0).state
# → {'module': '__main__', 'class': 'Scale', 'config': {'factor': 2.0}}
pk.loads(pk.dumps(Scale(2.0)))   # → Scale(factor=2.0)

docs.title: Sequential
docs.text:
Apply operators left to right. It checks at construction that every item is an operator and that a _terminal one comes last; | flattens, so (a | b) | c and a | (b | c) are the same three steps. It has len, indexing and slicing, a Keras-style summary(signature) and a describe() tree, and the empty Sequential is the identity.

from pipekit import Sequential, Signature

pipe = Scale(0.5) | Scale(2.0) | Scale(3.0)
pipe(10.0)         # → 30.0
len(pipe)          # → 3
pipe[1:]           # → Sequential([Scale(factor=2.0), Scale(factor=3.0)])
Sequential([])(7)  # → 7

print(pipe.summary(Signature(dims=(("y", 4), ("x", 4)), dtype="float32")))
# Operator   Input sig                      Output sig
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# [0] Scale  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)
# [1] Scale  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)
# [2] Scale  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)  Signature((y=4, x=4) float32)

docs.title: Graph, Input and Node
docs.text:
For flows that branch and merge, with several inputs and named outputs. Calling operators on Inputs (and on what those calls return) records the graph; Graph(inputs=…, outputs=…) wraps it, rejects cycles, and evaluates in topological order. Inputs bind by keyword or by position; outputs come back as a dict.

from pipekit import Graph, Input, Lambda

a, b = Input("a"), Input("b")
s = Scale(2.0)(a)                                     # s = 2a
total = Lambda(lambda u, v: u + v, name="add")(s, b)  # s + b

g = Graph(inputs={"a": a, "b": b}, outputs={"s": s, "sum": total})
g(a=1.0, b=10.0)   # → {'s': 2.0, 'sum': 12.0}
g(1.0, 10.0)       # → the same; positional arguments bind in declaration order

A single-input graph composes into a Sequential ((Scale(2.0) | g1)(1.0) → {'y': 6.0} for a graph g1 with output y = 3x). The bigger-graph tutorial builds a full one.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Free functions that carry the toolz surface. They are not operators themselves (except what they return). Below, inc = Lambda(lambda v: v + 1).

Function toolz ancestor What it does Example pipe(value, *ops) toolz.pipe Sequential(ops)(value) compose(*ops) toolz.compose right to left: compose(f, g, h) is Sequential([h, g, f]) compose(Scale(2.0), inc)(3.0) → 8.0 compose_left(*ops) toolz.compose_left left to right, like Sequential compose_left(Scale(2.0), inc)(3.0) → 7.0 juxt(*ops) toolz.juxt each operator on the same input; a tuple juxt(Identity(), Scale(2.0))(5.0) → (5.0, 10.0) complement(pred) toolz.complement negates a predicate complement(str.isdigit)("a") → True

juxt returns a plain function, so it cannot sit inside a Sequential; Fanout is the operator-shaped version.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
Operator Purpose Holds a closure Identity() an explicit no-op; the default branch of Branch and Switch no Const(value) return a fixed value, whatever the input no Lambda(fn, name=…) wrap any callable; the escape hatch yes Sink(write_fn, name=…) write as a side effect, return the input unchanged yes

Sink returns its input, so a pipeline can continue past it. An operator that really ends a pipeline (writes and returns nothing) sets _terminal = True.

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
Decisions and failures as steps inside the pipeline, rather than if and try around it.

Operator Purpose Branch(predicate, if_true, if_false=Identity()) a binary choice Switch(key, cases, default=Identity()) dispatch on key(carrier) Try(primary, fallback, on) run fallback when primary raises one of on Coalesce(sources, is_ok, on=()) the first source whose output passes is_ok Retry(op, attempts, base_delay, on) retry on on; attempt i waits base_delay · 2^(i−1) 
from pipekit import Coalesce, Const, Lambda, Retry, Try


def down(_):
    raise IOError("down")


Try(Lambda(down), Const(0.0), on=(IOError,))(1.0)    # → 0.0
Coalesce(
    [Lambda(down), Const(-1), Const(5)],
    is_ok=lambda r: r > 0,                            # -1 fails the check
    on=(IOError,),                                    # down() falls through
)(0)                                                  # → 5
Retry(flaky, attempts=5, base_delay=0.0, on=(ConnectionError,))(42)
# → 42, where flaky is an operator that raises ConnectionError twice, then succeeds

Try and Retry require their exception list, so neither is ever a silent catch-all; when every source fails, Coalesce raises RuntimeError. The ETL tutorial nests all three around a reader.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
The carrier flows through unchanged; something useful happens on the side.

Name Purpose Tap(fn, name=…) call fn on the carrier; return the carrier Snapshot() + .at(key) capture intermediates by name in snapshot.captures ShapeTrace(printer=print, mode="every" \| "diff_only", label=None, extra=None) log shape and dtype at each step; extra(carrier) adds a line (a coordinate system, units) Profile() + .wrap(op) time each call; profile.report() gives calls, total and mean per operator Histogram(bins=10, to_array=list) + .at(key) capture distributions; to_array turns the carrier into numbers

Snapshot, Profile and Histogram are controllers, not operators: the operators you place in the pipeline come from .at() and .wrap(), and the data they collect lives on the controller.

from pipekit import Histogram, Lambda, Profile, Snapshot

snap, prof, hist = Snapshot(), Profile(), Histogram(bins=2)
pipe = Lambda(lambda v: [v, 2 * v], name="pair") | snap.at("mid") | hist.at("out")
pipe(1.0)                   # → [1.0, 2.0]
snap.captures               # → {'mid': [1.0, 2.0]}
prof.wrap(Scale(3.0))(2.0)  # → 6.0;  prof.report() → {'Scale': {'calls': 1.0, ...}}

docs.title: Combination
docs.text:
Fanout runs several operators on the same input and returns a dict of their outputs:

from pipekit import Fanout, Lambda

Fanout({"n": Lambda(len), "u": Lambda(str.upper)})("ab")   # → {'n': 2, 'u': 'AB'}

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Cache(inner) (alias Memoize) memoises an operator in memory, keyed by a SHA-256 of the input and the inner operator's configuration. Arrays are keyed by their bytes, dtype and shape, so two large arrays never collide, and the bookkeeping is thread-safe, so one Cache can be shared by ThreadMap workers.

from pipekit import Cache, Memoize

c = Cache(Scale(2.0))
c(1.0); c(1.0); c(2.0)
c.hits, c.misses    # → (1, 2)
Memoize is Cache    # → True

docs.title: Quality control
docs.text:
Assertions as pass-through operators: a research-time "this won't break" becomes a permanent guard.

Operator Purpose Holds a closure Quarantine(check, sentinel, on_quarantine=None) on failure call on_quarantine and return sentinel; never raises yes AssertShape(expected_shape) raise QCError on a shape mismatch; None matches any size no AssertDType(expected_dtype) raise QCError on a dtype mismatch no AssertHasAttribute(name, value=…) raise QCError if an attribute is missing or wrong no AssertCallable(predicate, message=…) raise QCError if a predicate fails yes 
AssertShape((2, 4))(x)   # x.shape == (2, 3)
# QCError: AssertShape: axis 1 expected 4, got 3 (expected=(2, 4), actual=(2, 3)).

The checks read shape, dtype and attributes and never look inside the data, so they work on any carrier. QCError subclasses AssertionError. Quarantine is the batch-friendly one: the inference and ETL tutorials use it to set bad records aside and keep going.

docs.title: Shape inference
docs.text:
Signature is an immutable record of named dimensions and a dtype; a size of None marks a dimension dynamic. An operator declares how it changes a signature by overriding compute_output_signature; returning None means "this operator does not track shape", and Sequential.summary shows ? for it.

from pipekit import Signature

sig = Signature(dims=(("time", 12), ("y", 256), ("x", 256)), dtype="float32")
sig.format()                  # → '(time=12, y=256, x=256) float32'
sig.drop_dims(("time",))      # → Signature((y=256, x=256) float32)
sig.replace_dims({"x": 128})  # → Signature((time=12, y=256, x=128) float32)

Containers report what they return: - Cache, Retry and Profile.wrap report their inner operator's signature. - Try, Branch, Switch and Coalesce report the signature their branches agree on, else None. - Fanout and the parallel maps report None, because they return a dict or a list.

A Graph propagates signatures node by node: output_signatures gives each output's, and summary prints the table. A node with several inputs gets its operator's signature only when the inputs agree; otherwise it shows ?:

from pipekit import Graph, Input, Operator


class MeanOver(Operator):
    """Mean over one named dimension: drops it from the signature."""

    def __init__(self, dim: str) -> None:
        self.dim = dim

    def _apply(self, x):
        return x.mean(axis=0)

    def compute_output_signature(self, signature):
        return None if signature is None else signature.drop_dims((self.dim,))


x = Input("x")
g = Graph(inputs={"x": x}, outputs={"climatology": MeanOver("time")(x)})
print(g.summary(sig))
# Node                 Input sig                        Output sig
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# [0] MeanOver(x)      (time=12, y=256, x=256) float32  (y=256, x=256) float32
# → climatology = [0]                                   (y=256, x=256) float32

The payoff grows as the operators you write (and domain libraries) declare theirs.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text:
Four shapes, one wrapper each. Every wrapper takes an iterable and returns a list in input order.

Shape When Constraint Operator Threads I/O-bound: object-store reads, downloads the I/O must release the GIL ThreadMap(op, n_workers=8) Processes CPU-bound work every step must pickle ProcessMap(op, n_workers=8, on_error="raise" \| "log_and_continue") Async I/O on one thread: web services async def _apply, or a sync operator run in a thread AsyncMap(op, semaphore=8) Batches GPU inference, vectorised code the inner operator takes a list of items BatchedMap(op, batch_size=8, flatten=True) 
from pipekit import AsyncMap, BatchedMap, Lambda, ThreadMap

ThreadMap(Scale(2.0), n_workers=2)([1, 2, 3])             # → [2.0, 4.0, 6.0]
add_up = Lambda(lambda b: [sum(b)], name="sum")
BatchedMap(add_up, batch_size=2)([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])         # → [3, 7, 5]
AsyncMap(Scale(2.0), semaphore=2)([1, 2])                 # → [2.0, 4.0]

Pickling. Process pools need every operator to pickle, and closures (Lambda, Tap, Sink, a Branch predicate), open handles and captured random generators do not. Operators that hold a closure carry forbid_in_yaml = True, and check_pickleable(op) walks a whole pipeline, however deeply nested, and returns the flagged operators before you fan out:

from pipekit import Branch, Cache, Identity, Tap, ThreadMap, check_pickleable

pipe = ThreadMap(Cache(Scale(2.0) | Tap(print) | Branch(bool, Identity())))
[type(op).__name__ for op in check_pickleable(pipe)]   # → ['Tap', 'Branch']

Async. AsyncMap(...)(items) drives its own event loop, so it works in scripts. Inside a running loop (a FastAPI or LitServe handler) it raises a RuntimeError that says to await its run method instead:

async def handler(items):
    return await AsyncMap(Scale(2.0)).run(items)   # → [2.0, 4.0] for [1, 2]

Deliberately left out. No automatic parallelism (Sequential is sequential; Graph evaluates in one process), no backend abstraction (the wrappers are concurrent.futures and asyncio), no fault tolerance beyond on_error="log_and_continue", and no distributed execution: Dask, Ray, Beam and orchestrators schedule pipekit operators; pipekit keeps them pickleable so they can.

docs.title: Serialisation
docs.text:
Name What it does dumps(op) JSON-encode op.state, keys sorted, nested operators included loads(s) rebuild the whole tree through Operator.from_state; the defining modules must be imported register(cls) add a class to the sandbox allowlist (also a class decorator) unregister(cls), allowed() remove from, and list, the allowlist loads_sandboxed(s) loads, but PermissionError for any class in the tree that is not registered from_state_sandboxed(state) the same check on a record already in memory

The sandboxed loader is for pipelines you did not write (uploaded by users, read from a queue): only classes you registered can be built, at any depth, and every class is checked before anything is constructed. Nothing is allowed by default, pipekit's own containers included.

import pipekit as pk

pk.dumps(pk.Const(3))
# → '{"class": "Const", "config": {"value": 3}, "module": "pipekit.blocks"}'
pk.loads(pk.dumps(Scale(2.0)))             # → Scale(factor=2.0)
pk.loads_sandboxed(pk.dumps(Scale(2.0)))   # PermissionError: not registered
pk.register(Scale)
pk.loads_sandboxed(pk.dumps(Scale(2.0)))   # → Scale(factor=2.0)
pk.loads(pk.dumps(pk.Lambda(abs)))         # RuntimeError: marked forbid_in_yaml

Nested pipelines round-trip too. A child operator appears in its parent's config as its own state record, a Graph records every node and its wiring, and an exception class (Try.on, Retry.on) is written as {"exception": "builtins.KeyError"}. pipeline_hash hashes that whole record, so two pipelines share a hash exactly when they are configured the same:

from pipekit import Cache, Retry, Sequential, ThreadMap, pipeline_hash

pipe = ThreadMap(Cache(Retry(Scale(2.0), attempts=3, base_delay=0.5, on=(OSError,))))
back = pk.loads(pk.dumps(pipe))
back.state == pipe.state                      # → True
pipeline_hash(back) == pipeline_hash(pipe)    # → True

pk.register(Sequential)
pk.loads_sandboxed(pk.dumps(Sequential([Scale(2.0), pk.Identity()])))
# PermissionError: '__main__.Scale' is not in the allowlist (checked first)

pipekit-experiment's HydraConfigLoader does the same with _target_ YAML: to_yaml(op) writes any pipeline, from_yaml loads it through Hydra, and from_yaml_sandboxed loads untrusted YAML through the allowlist without ever calling Hydra's instantiate.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Most operators are stateless: _apply(carrier) → carrier. Some work carries state from call to call: a data-assimilation cycle (forecast, analysis, forecast…), a training loop (optimiser state, step, metrics), a streaming statistic, a recurrent model. A StatefulOperator implements _apply(carrier, state) → (carrier, state), and a CarryState is the base for that state, with to_dict / from_dict for checkpointing. A Sequential that contains a stateful step threads the state through and returns (carrier, state); stateless steps pass it along untouched.

A streaming mean: after values x₁, …, xₙ the state is the running sum Sₙ = ∑ᵢ xᵢ = Sₙ₋₁ + xₙ and the count n, and the step emits x̄ₙ = Sₙ / n.

from pipekit import CarryState, StatefulOperator


class MeanState(CarryState):
    def __init__(self, total: float, n: int) -> None:
        self.total = total  # Sₙ = ∑ᵢ xᵢ
        self.n = n          # n


class StreamMean(StatefulOperator):
    def _apply(self, x, state):
        st = MeanState(state.total + x, state.n + 1)  # Sₙ = Sₙ₋₁ + xₙ;  n ← n + 1
        return st.total / st.n, st                    # x̄ₙ = Sₙ / n


pipe = Scale(1.0) | StreamMean()                    # a stateless step, then a stateful one
x_bar, st = pipe(4.0, state=MeanState(0.0, 0))      # x̄₁ = 4.0
x_bar, st = pipe(8.0, state=st)                     # x̄₂ = 6.0
st                                                  # → MeanState(total=12.0, n=2)
MeanState.from_dict(st.to_dict()) == st             # → True
pipe(4.0)   # TypeError: ... called without a `state` argument

A Graph threads state the same way. Call it with state= and it returns (outputs, state); the state passes through its stateful nodes in topological order (the order describe() lists):

from pipekit import Graph, Input

x = Input("x")
g = Graph(inputs={"x": x}, outputs={"mean": StreamMean()(Scale(1.0)(x))})
out, st = g(x=4.0, state=MeanState(0.0, 0))   # out == {"mean": 4.0}
out, st = g(x=8.0, state=st)                  # out == {"mean": 6.0}

pipekit-cycle's Cycle, DACycle and EnsembleDACycle and pipekit-train's TrainingLoop are built on these two classes; see the data-assimilation and training tutorials.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text: Model wrappers in the sister libraries rely on two duck-typed seams, written down once as runtime_checkable Protocols: Predictor (anything with predict(x)) and FittableTransformer (anything with fit(x) and transform(x)). isinstance(model, Predictor) checks that the methods exist, not their signatures, so a scikit-learn estimator, a JAX model wrapper or your own class all qualify without importing pipekit. The cycle and experiment packages define more such seams (ForwardModel, AnalysisStep, ModelRegistry, …); see Protocols.

docs.title: Limits today
docs.text:
The limits this page used to list have been fixed: - nested pipelines round-trip; - a Graph's state records every node, threads carry state and has a summary; - containers report the signature of what they return; - CarryState is consistently unhashable; - ProcessMap reports failures through logging; - AsyncMap explains itself inside a running loop; - ShapeTrace takes an extra line.

The design questions still open are tracked in the GeoStack design reports and pipekit's issues.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Five minutes from git clone to your first composed pipeline, first data-assimilation cycle, and first registered model. Pick the section that matches what you came for; you don't need to read them in order.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The fastest path — clone the workspace and sync:

git clone https://github.com/jejjohnson/pipekit.git
cd pipekit
uv sync --all-groups

Once any of the packages publish to PyPI, you install only what you need:

uv add pipekit                   # carrier-agnostic core only
uv add pipekit-cycle             # adds time-stepping / DA
uv add pipekit-train             # adds training pipelines
uv add 'pipekit-train[equinox]'  # plus the Equinox backend adapter

For the full per-package install matrix (every extra spelled out) see Installation.

docs.title: Your first pipeline
docs.text:
A pipeline is a chain of Operators. Compose them with |:

from pipekit import Operator, Tap


class Scale(Operator):
    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        self.factor = factor

    def _apply(self, x):
        return x * self.factor


pipe = Scale(2.0) | Tap(print, name="log") | Scale(3.0)
result = pipe(5.0)
# Prints: 10.0
# result == 30.0

The Tap is identity-with-side-effect — the carrier passes through unchanged, but print fires. Use it for logging, metrics, debug breakpoints. Sister: Sink (same machinery, different intent — persistence).

For non-linear flows use Graph with named nodes; see Concepts.

docs.title: Your first DA cycle (pipekit-cycle)
docs.text:
A forecast-only loop:

import pipekit_cycle as pc


forecast = pc.Cycle(
    step_op=pc.CallableForward(my_step_fn, dt=3600.0),
    n_steps=24,
    save_history=True,
)
final_carrier, final_state = forecast(initial_carrier, initial_state)
trajectory = forecast.history  # list of (carrier, state) per saved step

A full data-assimilation cycle requires an algorithm library to satisfy the AnalysisStep protocol — for example filterx.adapters.pipekit.EnKFAnalysis. The pipekit-cycle side stays algorithm-agnostic:

from filterx.adapters.pipekit import EnKFAnalysis

da = pc.EnsembleDACycle(
    forward_model=my_forward_model,
    obs_op=pc.IdentityObs(),
    analysis_step=EnKFAnalysis(inflation=1.05),
    obs_source=my_obs_source_op,
    n_steps=24,
    n_members=40,
)
members, state = da(initial_members, pc.DAState(obs_err_cov=R))

The full walkthrough lives in tutorials/da-cycle.md.

docs.title: Your first trained model (pipekit-train)
docs.text:
Train a tiny MLP regressor on synthetic data, end-to-end:

import jax
import equinox as eqx

from pipekit_train import IterableDataset, MSE, TrainingLoop
from pipekit_train.adapters.equinox import EquinoxModelOp


model_op = EquinoxModelOp(eqx.nn.MLP(
    in_size=1, out_size=1, width_size=16, depth=2, key=jax.random.key(0),
))

loop = TrainingLoop(
    model_op=model_op,
    dataset=my_dataset,                       # any TrainingDataset
    loss=MSE(),
    optimizer_config={"name": "adam", "learning_rate": 1e-2},
    max_steps=100,
    batch_size=16,
    backend="equinox",
    seed=42,
)

trained_op, artifact = loop.run()

trained_op is a pipekit.Operator that wraps the trained module; it composes into any Sequential / Graph / Cycle for inference. The artifact is a TrainingArtifact carrying the config hash, dataset hash, and registry URI (when wired to a ModelRegistry).

The full walkthrough lives in tutorials/train-emulator.md.

docs.title: Your first registry round-trip (pipekit-experiment)
docs.text:
Store a trained operator by content hash, retrieve it by hash or by tag:

import pipekit_experiment as pe


registry = pe.LocalModelRegistry("/tmp/models")

h = registry.store(
    trained_op,
    name="methane_emulator_v3",
    tags={"family": "methane"},
)

# Load by hash, or by tag name:
op_by_hash = registry.load(h)
op_by_tag = registry.load("methane_emulator_v3")

# Atomic tag promotion:
registry.tag(h, "production", force=True)

S3ModelRegistry (under the [s3] extra) is a drop-in replacement backed by fsspec.

docs.title: Closing the loop — train, register, deploy in a cycle
docs.text:
The reason the packages exist together: train a model in pipekit-train, register it via pipekit-experiment, drop it into a pipekit-cycle forecast as a NeuralForward, run a forecast that calls your trained model every step. The handoff is one operator swap — no rewrite.

import pipekit_cycle as pc
import pipekit_experiment as pe


# Train (see above) → register
h = registry.store(trained_op, name="surrogate_v1")

# Reload at deploy time → drop into a Cycle
op = registry.load(h)
forecast = pc.Cycle(
    step_op=pc.NeuralForward(op, dt=3600.0),
    n_steps=24,
)

This is the same Operator interface end-to-end. The full end-to-end notebook is at notebooks/pipekit_train_cycle_handoff.ipynb.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The full per-package install matrix. pipekit is a uv workspace — locally you sync the whole thing; once published, you install only the packages you need.

docs.title: Workspace install (recommended for development)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jejjohnson/pipekit.git
cd pipekit
uv sync --all-groups

This pulls every package, every dev tool, every dependency group. Everything works out of the box. Tests, docs, type-check, pre-commit hooks — all ready.

docs.title: Per-package install (production / end-user)
docs.text:
Once any of the packages publish to PyPI, you install only what you need:

uv add pipekit                    # core
uv add pipekit-cycle              # time-stepping + DA
uv add pipekit-experiment         # registry + tracker protocols
uv add pipekit-train              # training pipelines
uv add pipekit-array              # Array-API operators
uv add pipekit-jax                # JaxModelOp (Equinox round-trip)

pipekit-evaluate is pre-alpha: it ships the benchmark ladder, the Unit × Lens × Stage scorer taxonomy and the evaluation report.

docs.title: pipekit core
docs.text:
uv add pipekit

Pure Python; zero third-party dependencies. The composition primitives (Operator, Sequential, Graph, control flow, observation, parallel maps, caching, QC, YAML round-trip).

docs.title: pipekit-cycle
docs.text:
uv add pipekit-cycle

Depends on pipekit only. Time-stepping (Cycle, EnsembleCycle, WindowedCycle), DA cycles (DACycle, EnsembleDACycle, SmootherCycle), the three runtime-checkable protocols (ForwardModel, ObservationOperator, AnalysisStep) that algorithm libraries satisfy.

docs.title: pipekit-experiment
docs.text:
uv add pipekit-experiment              # registry + protocols + artifacts
uv add 'pipekit-experiment[dvc]'       # plus DVC adapter
uv add 'pipekit-experiment[hydra]'     # plus Hydra + hydra-zen
uv add 'pipekit-experiment[metaflow]'  # plus Metaflow @step wrapper
uv add 'pipekit-experiment[s3]'        # plus fsspec-backed S3ModelRegistry

Combine extras as needed:

uv add 'pipekit-experiment[dvc,hydra,metaflow,s3]'

The core surface (registry, protocols, artifacts) is importable even when no extras are installed. Each adapter raises a clean ImportError with the install hint on first use.

docs.title: pipekit-train
docs.text:
uv add pipekit-train                    # core training surface (no backend)
uv add 'pipekit-train[equinox]'         # Equinox + Optax + Grain + Orbax adapter
uv add 'pipekit-train[lightning]'       # Lightning adapter (v0.2 — pending)
uv add 'pipekit-train[keras]'           # Keras 3 adapter (v0.3 — pending)
uv add 'pipekit-train[cycle]'           # SimulationDataset over pipekit-cycle
uv add 'pipekit-train[experiment]'      # LogToExperiment callback
uv add 'pipekit-train[cache]'           # local-fs CachedDataset (zarr)
uv add 'pipekit-train[s3]'              # cloud-fs CachedDataset (zarr + fsspec)
uv add 'pipekit-train[gcs]'             # GCS variant

(A [catalog] extra for geocatalog CatalogDataset support is documented in the pipekit-train design but lands only once geocatalog publishes to PyPI; it isn't declared in pyproject.toml today.)

Typical combo for a JAX user shipping reproducible training:

uv add 'pipekit-train[equinox,experiment,cycle]'

docs.title: pipekit-array
docs.text:
uv add pipekit-array            # operators only (raises at call if no backend)
uv add 'pipekit-array[numpy]'   # numpy >= 2.0
uv add 'pipekit-array[jax]'     # jax >= 0.4.20
uv add 'pipekit-array[torch]'   # torch >= 2.0 (needs [compat])
uv add 'pipekit-array[cupy]'    # cupy >= 13
uv add 'pipekit-array[dask]'    # dask[array] >= 2024 (partial conformance)

The default install brings nothing — operators raise TypeError at call time if the input doesn't implement the Array API. Recommended minimal install is pipekit-array[numpy].

For PyTorch you need both extras:

uv add 'pipekit-array[torch,compat]'

array-api-compat is required because PyTorch tensors don't expose __array_namespace__ natively.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
The shapes real pipelines take once they leave the notebook, which pipekit pieces each one uses, and what is still missing.

About this page Covers Fourteen deployment patterns and four habits that cut across them Read first A tour of the core Worked examples The tutorials, linked from each pattern History Distilled from Report 9 of the GeoStack design reports, which walks twenty cases through one domain (a methane plume from a satellite scene) and now points here

A pipeline is written once and then used in many places: a notebook, a batch job, a web service, a scheduled family of runs, an audit. pipekit's bet is that these are the same object in different harnesses, so the patterns below are mostly about which harness to put around an Operator, and which of its properties (a config, a hash, pickleability) the harness relies on.

Each pattern names its pipekit pieces, says what works today and what does not, and links the tutorial that runs it end to end. The status column uses three marks: today (ships and is tested), partly (works with a workaround), missing (needs code that does not exist yet).

# Pattern Pieces Status Tutorial 1 Explore, then batch Tap, ShapeTrace, Profile, Snapshot today bigger graph 2 ETL over many inputs ProcessMap, Quarantine, Sink today ETL over many regions 3 Validation as operators Assert*, Quarantine, QCError today inference 4 Fusing several inputs Graph, Input today bigger graph 5 One preprocessing object for training and serving Operator config, registry today train, register, forecast 6 Cycles: time stepping and assimilation StatefulOperator, pipekit-cycle today DA cycle, ensemble DA 7 An inference service AsyncMap.run, BatchedMap, the config hash today inference 8 Promotion by tag LocalModelRegistry.tag today — 9 Pipelines from users register, loads_sandboxed, from_yaml_sandboxed today — 10 A pinned artifact InferenceArtifact, TrainingArtifact, to_yaml today — 11 Orchestrator tasks with deterministic keys pipeline_hash today ETL over many regions 12 A/B comparison Fanout partly — 13 Scheduled families, backfills and what-if reruns the config hash today — 14 The feedback loop pipekit-train, registry today train, register, forecast

The snippets share one small operator, a detector with a threshold:

from pipekit import Operator


class Threshold(Operator):
    """x ↦ 1[x > k]."""

    def __init__(self, *, k: float) -> None:
        self.k = k

    def _apply(self, x):
        return x > self.k

docs.title: 1. Explore, then batch
docs.text:
The problem. A pipeline grows in a notebook, one step at a time, with prints and plots between the steps. Then it has to run on a thousand inputs, and the prints and plots have to go.

The pattern. Observers pass their input through unchanged, so you can leave them in while you explore and drop them, or point them at a logger, when you batch. ShapeTrace logs each step's shape and dtype, Profile times a step, Snapshot keeps a copy of an intermediate, and Tap calls any function on it. The object you explored with is the object you batch.

from pipekit import Profile, ShapeTrace, Snapshot, Tap

snap, prof = Snapshot(), Profile()
explore = (
    clean | ShapeTrace() | snap.at("clean")   # log shape and dtype, keep a copy
    | features | Tap(plot)                    # look at the features
    | prof.wrap(model)                        # time the model
)
batch = clean | features | model             # the same steps, no observers
snap.captures["clean"], prof.report()        # what the exploration saw

Today. All of it. ShapeTrace(extra=...) adds a line for whatever else a carrier carries (units, a coordinate system).

docs.title: 2. ETL over many inputs
docs.text:
The problem. One pipeline, many inputs (regions, files, stations, days), some of them broken in ways you only find at scale.

The pattern. Extract with a list of keys, transform with ProcessMap(pipeline, on_error="log_and_continue") so one bad input leaves a None instead of killing the run, set malformed records aside with Quarantine, and load with a Sink that writes one keyed output per input. Run check_pickleable(pipeline) before fanning out: closures do not cross process boundaries.

Today. All of it. log_and_continue reports each failure as a warning, with its traceback, on the pipekit.parallel logger, so the run's logging setup decides where failures go.

docs.title: 3. Validation as operators
docs.text:
The problem. Checks scattered through glue code are skipped, duplicated, or run in the wrong place.

The pattern. A check is a step. AssertShape, AssertDType, AssertHasAttribute and AssertCallable raise QCError when an input is wrong; Quarantine(check, sentinel, on_quarantine) replaces a bad input with a sentinel and hands it to a callback, for streams where one bad record should not stop the rest. Put the hard checks at the boundaries (after loading, before the model, before writing) and the soft ones on the records.

Today. All of it. Array-aware checks (finite values, value ranges, across array libraries) are planned for pipekit-array; until then AssertCallable takes any predicate.

docs.title: 4. Fusing several inputs
docs.text:
The problem. A product needs two or more sources at once: two sensors, a measurement and a reference, a feed and its timestamp.

The pattern. A Graph. Each source is an Input, each step is called on the nodes it needs, and the outputs are named. Steps that take two carriers (_apply(self, a, b)) are ordinary operators.

from pipekit import Graph, Input

a, b = Input("a"), Input("b")
fused = Align()(a, b)
g = Graph(inputs={"a": a, "b": b}, outputs={"product": Model()(fused)})
g(a=scene_a, b=scene_b)["product"]

Today. All of it, stateful steps included: call the graph with state= and it returns (outputs, state). Shape inference stops at the graph's edge.

docs.title: 5. One preprocessing object for training and serving
docs.text:
The problem. Training normalises with one piece of code and serving with another, and they drift: the classic train/serve skew.

The pattern. The fitted preprocessing is an operator whose fitted values (a mean, a standard deviation, a vocabulary) are its configuration. Store it in the registry next to the model, with its hash in the model's tags, and load both by name at serving time. There is then exactly one Standardize(mean=…, std=…) in the world, and the hash proves which one ran.

scaler_hash = registry.store(scaler, name="scaler")
registry.store(model, name="model", weights=blob, tags={"scaler": scaler_hash})

serve = registry.load("scaler") | model_template.with_weights(
    registry.load_weights("model")
)

Today. All of it (LocalModelRegistry, S3ModelRegistry, JaxModelOp.with_weights). The tutorial fits the scaler on the training split only, so validation never sees its statistics.

docs.title: 6. Cycles: time stepping and assimilation
docs.text:
The problem. Forecast, observe, correct, repeat: the carrier is a state, and every step needs the previous one.

The pattern. pipekit-cycle. A Cycle steps a forward model; a DACycle or EnsembleDACycle alternates forecast and analysis, with observation operators and noise models as Protocols, so the filter can come from any library. Pre-processing (quality control, thinning, unit conversion of the observations) and post-processing (verification, spread–skill) are ordinary operators around the cycle.

Today. All of it.

docs.title: 7. An inference service
docs.text:
The problem. A web handler receives a request, runs a pipeline and must say exactly what produced its answer.

The pattern. Build the pipeline once at start-up. Inside the handler, which already runs in an event loop, use await AsyncMap(op).run(items) (not AsyncMap(op)(items), which starts its own loop). Batch for a GPU with BatchedMap, or let the model batch. Return the pipeline's content hash with every answer, so a response can be traced to a configuration.

Today. All of it. pipekit provides no server: LitServe, FastAPI or anything else hosts the operator.

docs.title: 8. Promotion by tag
docs.text:
The problem. Several candidate versions exist; one of them is "the" model that serving uses, and promoting a new one (or rolling back) must not need a redeploy.

The pattern. Store every candidate by content hash; point a human-readable tag at the one in service. Serving loads by tag; promotion and rollback move the tag. The same configuration always gets the same hash, so storing it twice is harmless.

import tempfile
from pipekit_experiment import LocalModelRegistry

registry = LocalModelRegistry(tempfile.mkdtemp())
v1 = registry.store(Threshold(k=3.0), name="detector-candidate")
v2 = registry.store(Threshold(k=2.5), name="detector-candidate")

registry.tag(v1, "detector", force=True)   # v1 in service
registry.tag(v2, "detector", force=True)   # promote v2
registry.load("detector")                  # → Threshold(k=2.5)
registry.tag(v1, "detector", force=True)   # roll back
registry.store(Threshold(k=3.0)) == v1     # → True: same config, same hash

Today. All of it.

docs.title: 9. Pipelines from users
docs.text:
The problem. Users (or another team, or a queue) send pipelines as data. Building arbitrary classes from a string is code execution.

The pattern. Register the classes you allow, containers included, and build untrusted input with loads_sandboxed (JSON) or HydraConfigLoader.from_yaml_sandboxed (_target_ YAML). Every class in the tree is checked before anything is built, and anything unregistered raises PermissionError. Operators holding closures are forbid_in_yaml and never deserialise, registered or not.

import pipekit as pk
from pipekit_experiment.adapters.hydra import HydraConfigLoader

pk.register(pk.Sequential)
pk.register(Threshold)

text = """
_target_: pipekit.Sequential
operators:
  - _target_: __main__.Threshold
    k: 2.0
"""
# a Sequential holding Threshold(k=2.0)
detector = HydraConfigLoader.from_yaml_sandboxed(text)

The YAML loader never calls Hydra's instantiate, which would call any dotted path (_target_: os.system): it translates the YAML into a state record and builds that through the allowlist. Interpolations (${...}) are not resolved, so a sandboxed config cannot read the environment.

Today. All of it.

docs.title: 10. A pinned artifact
docs.text:
The problem. A result has to be reproducible months later, for a review, an audit or a paper: the exact pipeline, the exact weights, the exact dependencies.

The pattern. pipekit-experiment's InferenceArtifact(pipeline_yaml, pinned_model_hashes, backend_info, deps_lock, metadata) records what ran; TrainingArtifact records how the model was made (the training pipeline, the dataset's hash, the model's hash, the tracker run). Keep the artifact with the output.

For the pipeline_yaml field, HydraConfigLoader.to_yaml(pipeline) writes the pipeline that actually ran, however deeply nested, and from_yaml loads it back with the same state.

Today. All of it. TrainingLoop.run() returns a TrainingArtifact when pipekit-experiment is installed.

docs.title: 11. Orchestrator tasks with deterministic keys
docs.text:
The problem. An orchestrator (Prefect, Dagster, Airflow, a cron job) retries, resumes and backfills. Every task must know whether it has already run.

The pattern. One task is one operator call on one input. Its key is a hash of the operator's configuration and the input's identity, so a rerun with the same pipeline and input finds its output and skips; a change to either gives a new key.

from pipekit import pipeline_hash


def task_key(op: Operator, input_id: str) -> str:
    """One key per (pipeline configuration, input)."""
    return f"{pipeline_hash(op)[:16]}-{input_id}"


# the same pipeline on the same day: the same key, so the rerun skips
task_key(Threshold(k=3.0), "2026-10-16") == task_key(Threshold(k=3.0), "2026-10-16")
# one argument changed: a new key
task_key(Threshold(k=3.0), "2026-10-16") != task_key(Threshold(k=2.5), "2026-10-16")

Today. All of it. pipeline_hash hashes the whole configuration: every nested operator and, in a Graph, every node and its wiring. It is the hash the registry stores under, so a task key and a registry entry agree.

docs.title: 12. A/B comparison
docs.text:
The problem. A new pipeline version must be compared with the current one on the same inputs before it replaces it.

The pattern. Fanout({"a": current, "b": candidate}) runs both on each input and returns both outputs; a post-processing step compares them. Compare the distribution of the differences, not only their mean: two versions can agree on average and disagree badly on the inputs that matter.

from pipekit import Fanout

ab = Fanout({"a": Threshold(k=3.0), "b": Threshold(k=2.5)})
ab(2.8)   # → {'a': False, 'b': True}

Partly. The side-by-side run ships; a diff of two pipelines' configurations, and a report of where their outputs disagree, do not. pipekit-evaluate's scorers and EvaluationReport are the natural home.

docs.title: 13. Scheduled families, backfills and what-if reruns
docs.text:
The problem. The same pipeline runs every day (monitoring), over a past period (backfill), and again with one setting changed (what-if).

The pattern. Key every output by the pipeline's hash and the input's date or identity (pattern 11). A daily run and a backfill are the same task over different dates. A what-if is a new operator with one constructor argument changed, so it has a new hash and writes beside the original, never over it.

Today. All of it; the schedule belongs to the orchestrator.

docs.title: 14. The feedback loop
docs.text:
The problem. Reviewers accept or reject the pipeline's outputs, and those verdicts should improve the next model.

The pattern. Verdicts become labels; a frozen label set gets a content hash; pipekit-train's TrainingLoop trains on it and returns a TrainingArtifact; the new model is stored, compared with the current one (pattern 12) and promoted by tag (pattern 8). Every model can be traced back to the labels it saw.

Today. All of it, given a label store that hashes its frozen sets.

docs.title: Habits that cut across the patterns
Composition in the core, infrastructure next door
docs.text:
The core composes and nothing else; deployment infrastructure lives in the sister packages, each in one place.

Concern Lives in Operators, composition, parallel maps, nested JSON, the sandbox allowlist pipekit pipeline_hash and the hashing primitives pipekit.hashing Content-addressed storage, tags, artifacts, YAML loading pipekit-experiment Training loops and backends pipekit-train Time stepping and assimilation pipekit-cycle Benchmarks, scorers and reports pipekit-evaluate JAX models with weight round-trips pipekit-jax Domain operators, readers and writers your library, subclassing Operator

docs.title: Parallelism is chosen per deployment
docs.text:
Nothing is parallel by default; each deployment picks its primitive.

Deployment Primitive CPU-bound batch over many inputs ProcessMap I/O-bound reads ThreadMap I/O inside a running event loop (a server) await AsyncMap(op).run(items) GPU inference BatchedMap, or the model batches Across machines the orchestrator, calling pickleable operators

docs.title: YAML is the shared language, both ways
docs.text: Every operator, in any library, subclasses Operator, so a Hydra YAML with _target_ paths can name steps from several libraries side by side. HydraConfigLoader.from_yaml builds the nested pipeline, to_yaml writes one built in Python, and from_yaml_sandboxed loads YAML you did not write. A pipeline can start in Python or in YAML; either way the other form is one call away.

docs.title: JAX speeds the model, not the pipeline
docs.text: pipekit-jax wraps an Equinox model as an operator (JaxModelOp), with byte-identical weight round-trips through the registry, and adds diffrax forward models for pipekit-cycle. Inside the model, jit and vmap do their work; the pipeline around it stays eager Python. That is a deliberate split: pre- and post-processing are I/O and bookkeeping, where tracing buys little and costs flexibility.

docs.title: One domain, all the patterns
docs.text: The GeoStack design reports walk every pattern above through one example, a methane plume from a satellite scene: read the scene, retrieve the enhancement, detect the plume, estimate its emission rate, review it, and retrain. Report 9 has the twenty cases, the libraries each one needs, and the proposals that close the gaps marked partly and missing here.

docs.title: Protocols — the plug-in seam
docs.text:
pipekit's interoperability story is structural: algorithm and domain libraries plug in by satisfying a Protocol, never by inheriting from a pipekit base class or importing pipekit at all. Every protocol is @runtime_checkable, so isinstance(obj, ForwardModel) succeeds on any structurally compatible class — adapters in filterax, vardax, geotoolz, and xrtoolz stay dependency-free.

This page is the inventory: what each protocol is for, where it lives, and who satisfies it.

docs.title: Core (pipekit.protocols)
docs.text:
Carrier-agnostic seams for model-inference wrappers.

Protocol Contract Satisfied by Predictor predict(x) scikit-learn estimators, Keras models, geotoolz GeoTensorEstimator, xrtoolz XarrayEstimator FittableTransformer fit(x) + transform(x) scikit-learn transformers, the carrier-aware sklearn wrappers in geotoolz / xrtoolz

Models invoked via bare __call__ (PyTorch modules, JAX functions) are covered by callable(model) — a __call__-only Protocol would match nearly everything, so pipekit deliberately doesn't define one.

docs.title: The standard-form triple
docs.text:
Protocol Contract Role ForwardModel step(state, dt), dt, state_signature Advance the state — predict ObservationOperator __call__(state), linearize(state) State → predicted observations — compare AnalysisStep __call__(forecast, obs, *, obs_op, obs_err_cov) Forecast + observations → analysis — update

vardax exposes every Layer-2 method (OI, 3D-Var, strong/weak/incremental 4D-Var, FourDVarNet, amortized posteriors) as an AnalysisStep via .as_analysis_step(); its observation operators (LinearObs, MaskedIdentity, AveragingKernel) satisfy ObservationOperator directly.

docs.title: Reduced-order seams
docs.text: Protocol Contract Role ReducedBasis operg(t, X, state), prior_inv(X), nbasis Reduced control basis with a prior (4D-Var on SSH, …) TangentLinearModel tangent(state, dx, dt), adjoint(state, dz, dt) Explicit M′ / M* of the dynamics ErrorSubspace propagate(model, state, dt), modes, rank Propagating low-rank covariance factor (SEEK / SEIK) ReducedOrderModel encode, decode, step(coords, dt), latent_dim Galerkin ROM — projection maps + latent dynamics LatentMap encode(state), decode(coords) The stateless subset of ReducedOrderModel — what latent-space filters and autoencoder priors need

docs.title: Ensemble-method seams
docs.text:
Protocol Contract Role ObservationNoise covariance(), sample(key, shape) Error model usable by both deterministic and stochastic analyses CovarianceLocalizer __call__(covariance, coords) Distance-based covariance tapering (Gaspari-Cohn, …) EnsembleInflator __call__(particles, forecast_particles=None) Post-analysis inflation (multiplicative, RTPS / RTPP, additive)

filterax's AbstractNoise, AbstractLocalizer, and AbstractInflator hierarchies satisfy these structurally.

docs.title: Iterative-inversion seams
docs.text: Protocol Contract Role IterativeProcess init(particles, obs, noise_cov), update(state, forward_evals) Ensemble Kalman inversion / sampling (EKI, EKS, UKI) StepScheduler get_dt(state) Pseudo-time step policy for the process loop

docs.title: Experiment tracking (pipekit_experiment.protocols)
docs.text: Protocol Contract Satisfied by ExperimentTracker start_run, log_metrics, log_artifact, end_run MLflow / W&B / ClearML adapters, ad-hoc writers ModelRegistry store, load, list, tag LocalModelRegistry, S3ModelRegistry, MLflow-registry adapters

docs.title: Training (pipekit_train)
docs.text: Protocol Module Contract Loss pipekit_train.loss Carrier-agnostic loss callable Callback pipekit_train.callbacks Training-loop hook points MetricWriter pipekit_train.writer Metric sink (JSONLWriter is the reference impl)

docs.title: Benchmarking (pipekit_evaluate.benchmark.protocols)
docs.text: Protocol Contract Role Prior sample(n, key), log_prob(theta) Prior over task parameters θ Task name, domain, prior(), simulator(), observation_operator(), datasets() One benchmark scenario — reuses ForwardModel / ObservationOperator as its simulator Estimate point(), sample(n, key), log_prob(theta) A point and/or posterior produced by an estimator CovarianceEstimate Estimate + covariance() An estimate that reports its posterior covariance, for coverage and spread scorers Estimator rung, complexity, fit(task), __call__(obs) Any rung mapping observations → an Estimate Oracle reference_for(task) The designated reference estimator for a task Scorer name, __call__(prediction, reference); optional unit, lens, stages, differentiable tags, read by tags_of One (Unit, Lens) scorer — named metric values

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Protocols are minimal: only the members the consuming cycle or loop actually calls. Optional capabilities (e.g. ObservationOperator.linearize) may raise NotImplementedError.
  • runtime_checkable checks method presence, not signatures — treat isinstance as a structural sniff, not a type-safety guarantee.
  • Domain-specific interfaces stay in domain libraries: vardax keeps its Prior / GradModulator / CostFunction / Minimiser protocols, geotoolz keeps band resolution and tiled inference. Only seams shared by two or more consumers are promoted here.

docs.title: pipekit-array
docs.text:
Array-API operators on top of pipekit. One operator runs on numpy, JAX, CuPy, PyTorch, or dask via array_namespace(x) dispatch — see the design doc for the full architecture, ADRs, and the v0.1 operator catalogue.

Phase A of the v0.1 implementation has landed: namespace dispatch + reductions + stack/concat combinators. Phases B–D add geometry, QC, and the trained-model wrapper ModelOp.

docs.title: pipekit_array._namespace
docs.text:
Array API namespace dispatch shim.

The single point of backend dispatch for every pipekit-array operator. array_namespace(*xs) returns the Array API namespace (numpy, jax.numpy, torch via array-api-compat, …) shared by all input arrays.

Tries the optional array-api-compat library first — without it, PyTorch tensors don't expose __array_namespace__ natively and torch backends won't dispatch. Falls back to native x.__array_namespace__() lookup if the compat shim isn't installed.

See docs/design/architecture.md §4 and ADR A1 for the rationale.

docs.title: array_namespace(*xs)
docs.text:
Return the Array API namespace shared by all input arrays.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *xs Any

One or more array-like objects. All must share the same Array API backend.

()

Returns:

Type Description Any

The module-like namespace object (e.g. numpy, jax.numpy,

Any

array_api_compat.torch).

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If no input implements the Array API, or if the inputs span more than one backend. The error message is consistent whether or not array-api-compat is installed.

Source code in packages/pipekit-array/src/pipekit_array/_namespace.py 
def array_namespace(*xs: Any) -> Any:
    """Return the Array API namespace shared by all input arrays.

    Args:
        *xs: One or more array-like objects. All must share the same
            Array API backend.

    Returns:
        The module-like namespace object (e.g. `numpy`, `jax.numpy`,
        `array_api_compat.torch`).

    Raises:
        TypeError: If no input implements the Array API, or if the
            inputs span more than one backend. The error message is
            consistent whether or not `array-api-compat` is installed.
    """
    compat_ns = _compat_namespace()

    if compat_ns is not None:
        try:
            return compat_ns(*xs)
        except TypeError as exc:
            # array-api-compat's error messages differ from our
            # contract; re-raise with stable wording so tests and
            # users see a consistent shape.
            msg = str(exc)
            if "Multiple namespaces" in msg:
                names = sorted({type(x).__module__.split(".")[0] for x in xs})
                raise TypeError(_multi_backend_msg(names)) from exc
            raise TypeError(_NO_BACKEND_MSG) from exc

    namespaces: set[Any] = set()
    for x in xs:
        ns = getattr(x, "__array_namespace__", None)
        if ns is None:
            raise TypeError(
                f"Input of type {type(x).__name__!r} does not implement "
                f"the Array API (`__array_namespace__` missing). " + _NO_BACKEND_MSG
            )
        namespaces.add(ns())
    if len(namespaces) == 0:
        raise TypeError(_NO_BACKEND_MSG)
    if len(namespaces) > 1:
        names = sorted({ns.__name__ for ns in namespaces})
        raise TypeError(_multi_backend_msg(names))
    return next(iter(namespaces))

docs.title: pipekit_array.reductions
docs.text:
Reductions — MeanScalar.

Wraps xp.mean as a pipekit Operator. See docs/design/api/operators.md for the spec.

docs.title: MeanScalar
docs.text:
Bases: Operator

Reduce an array to a scalar (or per-axis means) via xp.mean.

Defaults to a full reduction (axis=None) yielding a scalar of rank 0. Output dtype matches the input's floating dtype per the Array API mean contract.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default axis int | tuple[int, ...] | None

Axis or tuple of axes to reduce over. None reduces all axes.

None keepdims bool

If True, retains the reduced axes with size 1.

False

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

From compute_output_signature when axis is out of range for the input signature's rank (xp.mean would raise the backend-native equivalent at apply time).

Example::

out = MeanScalar()(image)               # scalar
out = MeanScalar(axis=(-2, -1))(image)  # per-band mean
out = MeanScalar(axis=0, keepdims=True)(image)  # shape (1, H, W)
Source code in packages/pipekit-array/src/pipekit_array/reductions.py 
class MeanScalar(Operator):
    """Reduce an array to a scalar (or per-axis means) via `xp.mean`.

    Defaults to a full reduction (`axis=None`) yielding a scalar of
    rank 0. Output dtype matches the input's floating dtype per the
    Array API `mean` contract.

    Args:
        axis: Axis or tuple of axes to reduce over. `None` reduces
            all axes.
        keepdims: If True, retains the reduced axes with size 1.

    Raises:
        ValueError: From `compute_output_signature` when ``axis`` is out
            of range for the input signature's rank (``xp.mean`` would
            raise the backend-native equivalent at apply time).

    Example::

        out = MeanScalar()(image)               # scalar
        out = MeanScalar(axis=(-2, -1))(image)  # per-band mean
        out = MeanScalar(axis=0, keepdims=True)(image)  # shape (1, H, W)
    """

    #: saved states name the module it had before the rename (pipekit-array 0.0.3)
    __former_modules__: ClassVar[tuple[str, ...]] = ("pipekit_array.reduce",)

    def __init__(
        self,
        axis: int | tuple[int, ...] | None = None,
        keepdims: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        # a tuple of axes reloads from JSON as a list, which `xp.mean` rejects
        self.axis = tuple(axis) if isinstance(axis, list) else axis
        self.keepdims = keepdims

    def _apply(self, x: Any) -> Any:
        xp = array_namespace(x)
        return xp.mean(x, axis=self.axis, keepdims=self.keepdims)

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"axis": self.axis, "keepdims": self.keepdims}

    def compute_output_signature(self, input_signature: Any) -> Any:
        if input_signature is None:
            return None

        input_sig: Signature = input_signature
        n_dims = len(input_sig.dims)

        def _validate(axis: int) -> int:
            """Return positive axis index; raise on out-of-range."""
            if n_dims == 0 or axis < -n_dims or axis >= n_dims:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"MeanScalar.axis={axis!r} is out of range for input "
                    f"signature with {n_dims} dim(s); xp.mean would raise."
                )
            return axis % n_dims

        if self.axis is None:
            axes_to_reduce: tuple[int, ...] = tuple(range(n_dims))
        elif isinstance(self.axis, int):
            axes_to_reduce = (_validate(self.axis),)
        else:
            axes_to_reduce = tuple(_validate(a) for a in self.axis)

        if self.keepdims:
            new_dims = tuple(
                (name, 1) if i in axes_to_reduce else (name, size)
                for i, (name, size) in enumerate(input_sig.dims)
            )
        else:
            new_dims = tuple(
                (name, size)
                for i, (name, size) in enumerate(input_sig.dims)
                if i not in axes_to_reduce
            )
        return Signature(dims=new_dims, dtype=input_sig.dtype)

docs.title: pipekit_array.combinators
docs.text:
Combinators — StackAlong, ConcatenateAlong.

Thin wrappers over xp.stack and xp.concat (the Array API standardised names) so the operations compose into a pipeline. See docs/design/api/operators.md for the spec.

ApplyToBands lands in Phase B alongside BatchedMap.

docs.title: ConcatenateAlong
docs.text:
Bases: Operator

Concatenate a list-of-arrays along an existing axis via xp.concat.

xp.concat is the Array API standardised name; numpy 2.0+ exposes it as concat alongside the legacy concatenate alias. All input arrays must share shape (except along axis), dtype, and backend.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default axis int | None

Existing axis to concatenate along, for raw arrays. Default 0.

None dim str | None

For named carriers instead: the dim to join along (pipekit_array.concat). axis and dim are mutually exclusive.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

From _apply when the input sequence is empty (also via array_namespace when the inputs mix backends).

Example::

out = ConcatenateAlong(axis=0)([arr_a, arr_b])  # shape (2*N, H, W)
Source code in packages/pipekit-array/src/pipekit_array/combinators.py 
class ConcatenateAlong(Operator):
    """Concatenate a list-of-arrays along an existing axis via `xp.concat`.

    `xp.concat` is the Array API standardised name; numpy 2.0+
    exposes it as `concat` alongside the legacy `concatenate` alias.
    All input arrays must share shape (except along `axis`), dtype,
    and backend.

    Args:
        axis: Existing axis to concatenate along, for raw arrays. Default 0.
        dim: For named carriers instead: the dim to join along
            (`pipekit_array.concat`). ``axis`` and ``dim`` are mutually
            exclusive.

    Raises:
        ValueError: From ``_apply`` when the input sequence is empty
            (also via `array_namespace` when the inputs mix backends).

    Example::

        out = ConcatenateAlong(axis=0)([arr_a, arr_b])  # shape (2*N, H, W)
    """

    def __init__(self, axis: int | None = None, dim: str | None = None) -> None:
        if axis is not None and dim is not None:
            raise ValueError(
                "ConcatenateAlong takes axis= (raw arrays) or dim=, not both."
            )
        self.axis = 0 if axis is None and dim is None else axis
        self.dim = dim

    def _apply(self, xs: Sequence[Any]) -> Any:
        if len(xs) == 0:
            raise ValueError("ConcatenateAlong requires at least one input array.")
        if self.dim is not None:
            return dims.concat(list(xs), self.dim)
        xp = array_namespace(*xs)
        return xp.concat(list(xs), axis=self.axis)

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        if self.dim is not None:
            return {"dim": self.dim}
        return {"axis": self.axis}

All input arrays must share the same shape, dtype, and backend.

Position of the new axis in the output, for raw arrays. Default 0.

None dim str | None

Example::

out = StackAlong(axis=0)([arr_a, arr_b, arr_c])  # shape (3, H, W)
