class BatchedMap(Operator):
    """Split an iterable into batches and call ``op`` on each batch as a list.

    The carrier-agnostic batching primitive. The inner operator
    receives a *list* of items at a time; what it does with that list
    is its problem (vectorise, send to GPU, concatenate via
    ``np.stack``, …). Array-aware variants that split along axis 0 of
    a single array live in `pipekit-array`.

    Args:
        op: The inner `Operator` invoked per batch. It receives a
            ``list[item]`` and may return any value; the per-batch
            outputs are collected into a flat list if they're lists,
            otherwise appended as-is.
        batch_size: Maximum items per batch.
        flatten: If ``True`` (default) and every batch result is a
            list, the per-batch lists are concatenated. If ``False``,
            the per-batch results are returned as-is.

    Returns from ``__call__(iterable)``: a list — either of items
    (when ``flatten=True`` and the inner returns lists) or of batch
    outputs (otherwise).
    """

    __config_mixin_auto__ = False

    def __init__(
        self,
        op: Operator,
        batch_size: int = 8,
        flatten: bool = True,
    ) -> None:
        require_operator(op, "BatchedMap", "op")
        if batch_size < 1:
            raise ValueError(f"BatchedMap.batch_size must be >= 1, got {batch_size}.")
        self.op = op
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.flatten = flatten

    def _apply(self, iterable: Iterable[Any]) -> list[Any]:
        items = list(iterable)
        out: list[Any] = []
        for start in range(0, len(items), self.batch_size):
            batch = items[start : start + self.batch_size]
            result = self.op(batch)
            if self.flatten and isinstance(result, list):
                out.extend(result)
            else:
                out.append(result)
        return out

    def compute_output_signature(self, input_signature: Any) -> Any:
        """``None``: the output is a list of results, not one carrier."""
        return None

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "op": nested_config(self.op),
            "batch_size": self.batch_size,
            "flatten": self.flatten,
        }

class ProcessMap(Operator):
    """Apply ``op`` to each item of an iterable using a process pool.

    Use for CPU-bound, pickleable workloads. Every operator in the
    chain — and every closure inside it — must be pickleable.

    Args:
        op: The inner `Operator` invoked per item.
        n_workers: Maximum concurrent processes.
        on_error: ``"raise"`` (default) re-raises the first worker
            error; ``"log_and_continue"`` logs it as a warning on the
            ``pipekit.parallel`` logger (with the traceback) and
            substitutes ``None`` for the failing item.

    Returns from ``__call__(iterable)``: a list of results in input order.
    """

    __config_mixin_auto__ = False

    def __init__(
        self,
        op: Operator,
        n_workers: int = 8,
        on_error: str = "raise",
    ) -> None:
        require_operator(op, "ProcessMap", "op")
        if n_workers < 1:
            raise ValueError(f"ProcessMap.n_workers must be >= 1, got {n_workers}.")
        if on_error not in ("raise", "log_and_continue"):
            raise ValueError(
                "ProcessMap.on_error must be 'raise' or 'log_and_continue', "
                f"got {on_error!r}."
            )
        self.op = op
        self.n_workers = n_workers
        self.on_error = on_error

    def _apply(self, iterable: Iterable[Any]) -> list[Any]:
        items = list(iterable)
        with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=self.n_workers) as ex:
            futures = [ex.submit(self.op, item) for item in items]
            results: list[Any] = []
            for i, fut in enumerate(futures):
                try:
                    results.append(fut.result())
                except Exception as exc:
                    if self.on_error == "raise":
                        raise
                    log.warning(
                        "ProcessMap: item %d failed with %s: %s",
                        i,
                        type(exc).__name__,
                        exc,
                        exc_info=exc,
                    )
                    results.append(None)
            return results

    def compute_output_signature(self, input_signature: Any) -> Any:
        """``None``: the output is a list of results, not one carrier."""
        return None

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "op": nested_config(self.op),
            "n_workers": self.n_workers,
            "on_error": self.on_error,
        }

docs.text:
Return the list of forbid_in_yaml-flagged operators inside op.

Pre-deployment lint for ProcessMap shapes: any operator carrying forbid_in_yaml = True (closures, callables, user RNGs) is a pickleability hazard.

Walks the operator tree generically: every instance attribute of every operator is scanned for nested operators — held directly, inside list / tuple / set / dict containers, or inside Graph nodes — so new operator shapes are covered without registering their attribute names here. Returns the flagged operators in encounter order (deduplicated by id).

Source code in packages/pipekit/src/pipekit/parallel.py 
def check_pickleable(op: Operator) -> list[Operator]:
    """Return the list of `forbid_in_yaml`-flagged operators inside ``op``.

    Pre-deployment lint for `ProcessMap` shapes: any operator carrying
    ``forbid_in_yaml = True`` (closures, callables, user RNGs) is a
    pickleability hazard.

    Walks the operator tree generically: every instance attribute of
    every operator is scanned for nested operators — held directly,
    inside list / tuple / set / dict containers, or inside `Graph`
    nodes — so new operator shapes are covered without registering
    their attribute names here. Returns the flagged operators in
    encounter order (deduplicated by ``id``).
    """
    from pipekit._base.graph import Node

    found: list[Operator] = []
    seen: set[int] = set()

    def scan(value: Any) -> None:
        if isinstance(value, Operator):
            visit(value)
        elif isinstance(value, Node):
            if id(value) in seen:
                return
            seen.add(id(value))
            scan(value.operator)
            for parent in value.parents:
                scan(parent)
        elif isinstance(value, dict):
            for child in value.values():
                scan(child)
        elif isinstance(value, (list, tuple, set, frozenset)):
            for child in value:
                scan(child)

    def visit(node: Operator) -> None:
        if id(node) in seen:
            return
        seen.add(id(node))
        if getattr(type(node), "forbid_in_yaml", False):
            found.append(node)
        for value in vars(node).values():
            scan(value)

    visit(op)
    return found

docs.title: pipekit.serial
docs.text:
Group L — serialisation glue.

A small surface for JSON serialisation, plus a sandboxed loader for user-uploaded pipelines that only constructs operators registered in an allowlist.

  • dumps(op) -> str — JSON-encode op.state.
  • loads(s) -> Operator — round-trip via Operator.from_state. Any imported Operator subclass resolves, at any depth: a Sequential, Graph, Cache, Try, Fanout or parallel map comes back with its children. Operators that hold closures (forbid_in_yaml) refuse.
  • register(cls) — add an Operator subclass to the sandboxed loader's allowlist.
  • from_state_sandboxed(state) -> Operator — the same check on a state record already in memory (what other front ends, such as a YAML loader, build on).
  • loads_sandboxed(s) -> Operator — like loads but rejects any class, at any depth, not in the allowlist. Nothing is allowed by default, pipekit's own containers included: register Sequential, Graph, … as well as your steps. Use this for untrusted input (use case 6: user-uploaded pipelines).

YAML / Hydra loaders are intentionally not shipped here — they live in optional extras (pipekit[yaml], pipekit[hydra]).

See master plan Report 2, Group L.

def dumps(op: Operator) -> str:
    """JSON-encode an operator's state record.

    Round-trip: ``loads(dumps(op))`` reconstructs an operator with the
    same config, nested operators included. Operators with
    `forbid_in_yaml = True` emit debug-only payloads (their constructors
    need closures that aren't in the config), so ``loads`` refuses them
    with `RuntimeError`, wherever they sit in the tree.

    Args:
        op: The operator to encode.

    Returns:
        A JSON string suitable for round-trip via `loads`.

    Raises:
        TypeError: if ``op`` isn't an `Operator`.
    """
    if not isinstance(op, Operator):
        raise TypeError(f"dumps expects an Operator, got {type(op).__name__}.")
    return json.dumps(op.state, sort_keys=True)

def from_state_sandboxed(state: dict[str, Any]) -> Operator:
    """Build an operator tree from a state record, allowlisted classes only.

    The check behind `loads_sandboxed`, for a record already in memory
    (a YAML front end builds on it). Every class in the tree is checked
    before anything is built, so a refused pipeline constructs nothing.

    Raises:
        PermissionError: if any class in the tree isn't registered.
        ValueError / TypeError / RuntimeError: as `loads`.
    """
    module = state.get("module")
    cls = state.get("class")
    if not isinstance(module, str):
        raise ValueError(
            "loads_sandboxed: state must include a string `module` field, "
            f"got {type(module).__name__}."
        )
    if not isinstance(cls, str):
        raise ValueError(
            "loads_sandboxed: state must include a string `class` field, "
            f"got {type(cls).__name__}."
        )
    _check_allowed(state)
    return build_operator(state, _resolve_allowed)

def loads(s: str) -> Operator:
    """Decode an operator from its JSON state record.

    Resolves the target class via `Operator.from_state`, walking all
    imported subclasses. The caller must have imported the module
    declaring the target class — pipekit doesn't auto-import.

    Args:
        s: A JSON string produced by `dumps` (or compatible).

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the JSON is malformed.
        TypeError: if a named class isn't a loaded `Operator` subclass.
        RuntimeError: if a class in the tree is ``forbid_in_yaml``, or a
            config holds a value that is not JSON.
    """
    state = json.loads(s)
    if not isinstance(state, dict):
        raise ValueError(
            f"loads expects a JSON object encoding an operator state, "
            f"got a {type(state).__name__}."
        )
    return Operator.from_state(state)

def loads_sandboxed(s: str) -> Operator:
    """Like `loads`, but reject any class, at any depth, not in the allowlist.

    Use for untrusted input (user-uploaded pipelines, use case 6).
    Domain libraries register their operators via `register`; the
    sandboxed loader refuses to construct anything else. Every class in

    pipeline constructs nothing. Exception classes (`Try.on`,
    `Retry.on`) resolve only among already-imported modules.

def register(cls: type[Operator]) -> type[Operator]:
    """Register ``cls`` as loadable via `loads_sandboxed`.

    Idempotent — re-registering the same class is a no-op. The class
    must subclass `Operator`.

    Returns ``cls`` so the function doubles as a class decorator::

        @register
        class MyOp(Operator):
            ...
    """
    if not (isinstance(cls, type) and issubclass(cls, Operator)):
        raise TypeError(f"register requires an Operator subclass, got {cls!r}.")
    key = f"{cls.__module__}.{cls.__name__}"
    _ALLOWED[key] = cls
    return cls

docs.title: pipekit.state
docs.text:
Group M — state primitives.

Two primitives that enable stateful pipelines — the substrate for the pipekit-cycle sister package (time-stepping, DA cycles, iterative inference) and for the pipekit-train stateful trainer loop:

  • StatefulOperator — subclass marker. _apply has the signature (carrier, state) -> (carrier, state) instead of the stateless carrier -> carrier.
  • CarryState — base class for state threaded through a stateful pipeline. Subclasses define their own fields; the base provides JSON-roundtrip discipline (to_dict / from_dict).

Sequential detects when any of its operators is a StatefulOperator and threads state through automatically. Stateless operators in the chain pass state through unchanged. A Sequential containing only stateless operators behaves exactly as it did before this group landed.

Why this lives in pipekit core (not in pipekit-cycle):

  1. Sequential is defined here; its stateful-detection logic must be here too. Putting StatefulOperator in a sibling package would invert the dependency.
  2. Other sibling packages may want state — pipekit-train's TrainingLoop is itself stateful (optimizer / step / metrics threaded through epochs). Sharing the base class lets them all reuse the same plumbing.

See master plan Report 2, Group M.

docs.title: CarryState
docs.text:
Base class for state threaded through a stateful pipeline.

Concrete subclasses define their own fields — the base class intentionally does not dictate a schema. Different cycle patterns bring their own CarryState shape (pipekit-cycle.DAState, IterationState, WindowState, ...).

States compare by value (same type, same fields) but are not hashable: they are mutable (a stateful step may update one in place) and routinely hold arrays and dicts, so a value hash would be wrong after a mutation, or fail outright. Don't use a state as a dict key or a set member; key by something stable instead.

The base supplies JSON-roundtrip discipline:

  • to_dict returns the instance's __dict__ (so any attributes set in __init__ are captured).
  • from_dict reconstructs via cls(**d). Subclasses with non-trivial deserialisation override.

Subclassing pattern::

class IterationState(CarryState):
    def __init__(self, residual_norm: float, iter_count: int) -> None:
        self.residual_norm = residual_norm
        self.iter_count = iter_count

state = IterationState(residual_norm=1.0, iter_count=0)
state.to_dict()                  # {"residual_norm": 1.0, "iter_count": 0}
IterationState.from_dict(...)    # rebuilds

class CarryState:
    """Base class for state threaded through a stateful pipeline.

    Concrete subclasses define their own fields — the base class
    intentionally does not dictate a schema. Different cycle patterns
    bring their own ``CarryState`` shape (`pipekit-cycle.DAState`,
    `IterationState`, `WindowState`, ...).

    States compare by value (same type, same fields) but are not
    hashable: they are mutable (a stateful step may update one in
    place) and routinely hold arrays and dicts, so a value hash would be
    wrong after a mutation, or fail outright. Don't use a state as a dict
    key or a set member; key by something stable instead.

    The base supplies JSON-roundtrip discipline:

    - `to_dict` returns the instance's ``__dict__`` (so any attributes
      set in ``__init__`` are captured).
    - `from_dict` reconstructs via ``cls(**d)``. Subclasses with
      non-trivial deserialisation override.

    Subclassing pattern::

        class IterationState(CarryState):
            def __init__(self, residual_norm: float, iter_count: int) -> None:
                self.residual_norm = residual_norm
                self.iter_count = iter_count

        state = IterationState(residual_norm=1.0, iter_count=0)
        state.to_dict()                  # {"residual_norm": 1.0, "iter_count": 0}
        IterationState.from_dict(...)    # rebuilds
    """

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Return a dict of the instance's attributes."""
        return dict(vars(self))

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: dict[str, Any]) -> CarryState:
        """Reconstruct from ``to_dict`` output. Subclasses may override."""
        return cls(**data)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        fields = ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in vars(self).items())
        return f"{type(self).__name__}({fields})"

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if type(self) is not type(other):
            return NotImplemented
        return vars(self) == vars(other)

    # Mutable, compared by value: unhashable, as Python's own rule for
    # such classes has it (and as `extras` dicts made most states anyway).
    __hash__ = None  # type: ignore[assignment]

Marker base for operators whose _apply threads carry-state.

Subclasses implement _apply(carrier, state) -> (carrier, state) rather than the stateless (carrier,) -> carrier. The _is_stateful = True ClassVar flags the class so Sequential detects it and threads state through automatically.

Subclasses may set initial_state_fn to a callable () -> CarryState that produces a fresh initial state. This is used by pipekit-cycle's cycle wrappers to bootstrap iteration without forcing the caller to construct state explicitly.

Example::

class StreamMean(StatefulOperator):
    def __init__(self):
        self.initial_state_fn = lambda: MeanState(sum=0.0, n=0)

    def _apply(self, x, state):
        new = MeanState(sum=state.sum + x, n=state.n + 1)
        return new.sum / new.n, new

See pipekit-cycle (Report 10) for the cycle / DA wrappers built on this primitive.

Source code in packages/pipekit/src/pipekit/state.py 
class StatefulOperator(Operator):
    """Marker base for operators whose ``_apply`` threads carry-state.

    Subclasses implement ``_apply(carrier, state) -> (carrier, state)``
    rather than the stateless ``(carrier,) -> carrier``. The
    ``_is_stateful = True`` ClassVar flags the class so `Sequential`
    detects it and threads state through automatically.

    Subclasses may set ``initial_state_fn`` to a callable
    ``() -> CarryState`` that produces a fresh initial state. This is
    used by `pipekit-cycle`'s cycle wrappers to bootstrap iteration
    without forcing the caller to construct state explicitly.

    Example::

        class StreamMean(StatefulOperator):
            def __init__(self):
                self.initial_state_fn = lambda: MeanState(sum=0.0, n=0)

            def _apply(self, x, state):
                new = MeanState(sum=state.sum + x, n=state.n + 1)
                return new.sum / new.n, new

    See `pipekit-cycle` (Report 10) for the cycle / DA wrappers built
    on this primitive.
    """

    _is_stateful: ClassVar[bool] = True
    initial_state_fn: Callable[[], CarryState] | None = None

    def _apply(self, carrier: Any, state: Any) -> tuple[Any, Any]:  # type: ignore[override]
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"{type(self).__name__} must implement _apply(carrier, state)."
        )

docs.title: pipekit.protocols
docs.text:
Group N — carrier-agnostic structural protocols.

The duck-typed seams that model-inference wrappers across the sister libraries (geotoolz ModelOp, xrops ModelOp, xrsklearn SklearnOp, pipekit-jax JaxModelOp) all rely on, promoted to runtime-checkable Protocols so the contract is written down once instead of re-implied in each wrapper's docstring. Domain-specific protocols stay in their domain packages (pipekit_cycle.protocols, pipekit_experiment.protocols); this module holds only the carrier-agnostic ones.

runtime_checkable checks method presence, not signatures — an isinstance(model, Predictor) check is a structural sniff, not a guarantee that the call will succeed with your carrier.

Anything with sklearn-style fit + transform methods.

The split-object pattern's structural contract: an estimator that learns state from data (fit) and applies it (transform). scikit-learn transformers satisfy it as-is; the sister libraries' carrier-aware wrappers (GeoTensor / xarray marshalling) satisfy it by construction.

Members

fit(x): Learn internal state from x; return the fitted estimator (conventionally self). transform(x): Apply the learned state to x.

class FittableTransformer(Protocol):
    """Anything with sklearn-style ``fit`` + ``transform`` methods.

    The split-object pattern's structural contract: an estimator that
    learns state from data (``fit``) and applies it (``transform``).
    scikit-learn transformers satisfy it as-is; the sister libraries'
    carrier-aware wrappers (GeoTensor / xarray marshalling) satisfy it
    by construction.

    Members:
        fit(x): Learn internal state from ``x``; return the fitted
            estimator (conventionally ``self``).
        transform(x): Apply the learned state to ``x``.
    """

    def fit(self, x: Any) -> Any: ...

    def transform(self, x: Any) -> Any: ...

docs.title: pipekit.hashing
docs.text:
Stable hashing primitives shared across the workspace.

One canonical implementation of the content-hash building blocks that pipekit.Cache, pipekit_train.TrainingDataset.content_hash, and the content-addressed registries in pipekit_experiment all rely on. Before this module each of those sites carried its own copy of the same json.dumps(sort_keys=True, default=repr) + sha256 dance; keeping the primitives here means a framing change can never silently diverge between the cache key, the dataset hash, and the registry hash.

The helpers are deliberately tiny and dependency-free:

  • stable_json — deterministic JSON encoding (sorted keys, repr fallback for non-JSON values).
  • stable_repr — repr with a safe fallback for objects whose repr raises.
  • sha256_hex — hex digest over a sequence of chunks; callers control the framing (separators, optional parts) so existing digests stay byte-for-byte stable.
  • pipeline_hash — the content hash of a whole pipeline (and optional weights): the one the pipekit-experiment registries store under, and the key for anything that must recognise "the same pipeline again" (an orchestrator task, a cache, an artifact).

docs.title: pipeline_hash(op, weights=None)
docs.text:
Content hash of a pipeline's whole configuration, and optional weights.

sha256(stable_json(op.state) ‖ 0x00 ‖ weights). op.state records every nested operator and, for a Graph, every node and its wiring, so two pipelines get the same hash exactly when they are configured the same. It is the hash the pipekit-experiment registries store under, so registry.store(op) returns pipeline_hash(op).

Operators that hold closures (forbid_in_yaml) are hashed by their debug config, which names the callable but not its code: two different lambdas can share a hash.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default op Operator

The operator (or pipeline) to hash.

required weights bytes | None

Optional weight bytes; None and b"" hash alike.

None

Returns:

Type Description str

The 64-character lowercase hex digest.

Examples:

>>> from pipekit import Const
>>> pipeline_hash(Const(1)) == pipeline_hash(Const(1))
True
>>> pipeline_hash(Const(1)) == pipeline_hash(Const(2))
False
Source code in packages/pipekit/src/pipekit/hashing.py 
def pipeline_hash(op: Operator, weights: bytes | None = None) -> str:
    """Content hash of a pipeline's whole configuration, and optional weights.

    ``sha256(stable_json(op.state) ‖ 0x00 ‖ weights)``. ``op.state``
    records every nested operator and, for a `Graph`, every node and
    its wiring, so two pipelines get the same hash exactly when they
    are configured the same. It is the hash the pipekit-experiment
    registries store under, so ``registry.store(op)`` returns
    ``pipeline_hash(op)``.

    Operators that hold closures (``forbid_in_yaml``) are hashed by
    their debug config, which names the callable but not its code: two
    different lambdas can share a hash.

    Args:
        op: The operator (or pipeline) to hash.
        weights: Optional weight bytes; ``None`` and ``b""`` hash alike.

    Returns:
        The 64-character lowercase hex digest.

    Examples:
        >>> from pipekit import Const
        >>> pipeline_hash(Const(1)) == pipeline_hash(Const(1))
        True
        >>> pipeline_hash(Const(1)) == pipeline_hash(Const(2))
        False
    """
    return sha256_hex(stable_json(op.state), b"\x00", weights or b"")

docs.title: sha256_hex(*chunks)
docs.text:
Hex sha256 digest of the concatenated chunks.

String chunks are UTF-8 encoded; bytes chunks are hashed as-is. Callers own the framing — pass explicit separator chunks (e.g. b"\x00") between variable-length parts to avoid ambiguity.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *chunks bytes | str

The parts to fold into the digest, in order.

()

Returns:

Type Description str

The 64-character lowercase hex digest.

Source code in packages/pipekit/src/pipekit/hashing.py 
def sha256_hex(*chunks: bytes | str) -> str:
    """Hex sha256 digest of the concatenated ``chunks``.

    String chunks are UTF-8 encoded; bytes chunks are hashed as-is.
    Callers own the framing — pass explicit separator chunks (e.g.
    ``b"\\x00"``) between variable-length parts to avoid ambiguity.

    Args:
        *chunks: The parts to fold into the digest, in order.

    Returns:
        The 64-character lowercase hex digest.
    """
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    for chunk in chunks:
        h.update(chunk.encode("utf-8") if isinstance(chunk, str) else chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

def stable_json(obj: Any) -> str:
    """JSON-encode ``obj`` deterministically for hashing.

    Keys are sorted so dict ordering never changes the digest; values
    that are not JSON-serialisable fall back to ``repr``. The result is
    stable across processes for JSON-native payloads (the common case:
    ``Operator.get_config()`` dicts).

    Args:
        obj: Any value. Non-JSON values are encoded via ``repr``.

    Returns:
        The canonical JSON string.
    """
    return json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, default=repr)

def stable_repr(value: Any) -> str:
    """Return a stable string representation of ``value`` for hashing.

    Tries ``repr`` first; falls back to a type-name placeholder for
    objects whose ``repr`` raises. The result need not be reversible —
    only deterministic per-process for equal inputs.

    Args:
        value: Any value.

    Returns:
        ``repr(value)``, or ``"<unrepr TypeName>"`` if ``repr`` raises.
    """
    try:
        return repr(value)
    except Exception:
        return f"<unrepr {type(value).__name__}>"

docs.title: pipekit.testing
docs.text:
Contract checks for pipekit operators.

Call these from a library's test suite on every operator it ships:

  • assert_round_trip(op, *inputs) — the config round-trip contract (roadmap gate A1): loads(dumps(op)) has the same pipeline_hash and returns the same output on a fixed input.
  • public_operators(module) — every Operator subclass a module exports in its __all__, so a sweep can fail on an operator that has no test case yet.

Example::

from pipekit.testing import assert_round_trip

def test_scale_round_trips():
    assert_round_trip(Scale(factor=2.0), 3.0)

docs.title: assert_round_trip(op, *inputs, **kwargs)
docs.text:
Assert that op survives loads(dumps(op)) unchanged.

Checks, in order:

  1. dumps then loads rebuild an operator of the same class.
  2. The rebuilt operator has the same pipeline_hash, so its whole configuration (nested operators and Graph wiring included) came back.
  3. Called on the same inputs and kwargs, both operators return the same output. Comparison is exact: arrays (anything exposing __array__) must match in type, shape, dtype and bytes, so NaN equals NaN but -0.0 differs from 0.0; floats compare exactly (NaN equal to NaN); dicts (whatever their key order, as with ==), lists and tuples are compared item by item; any other value with ==. Array outputs need NumPy installed.

Both operators receive the same input objects: an operator that mutates its input breaks the carrier contract and may fail here.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default op Operator

The operator (or Sequential / Graph) under test.

required *inputs Any

Positional inputs for the call.

() **kwargs Any

Keyword inputs for the call (a Graph's named inputs).

{}

Returns:

Type Description Operator

The rebuilt operator, for further checks.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

if op, or any operator nested in it, is marked forbid_in_yaml (its config is a debug payload, so the round trip is not expected to hold).

AssertionError

on the first violated property, naming the operator.

Example::

>>> from pipekit import Const
>>> from pipekit.testing import assert_round_trip
>>> back = assert_round_trip(Const(3), "ignored")
>>> back.value
3
Source code in packages/pipekit/src/pipekit/testing.py 
def assert_round_trip(op: Operator, *inputs: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Operator:
    """Assert that ``op`` survives ``loads(dumps(op))`` unchanged.

    Checks, in order:

    1. ``dumps`` then ``loads`` rebuild an operator of the same class.
    2. The rebuilt operator has the same `pipeline_hash`, so its whole
       configuration (nested operators and `Graph` wiring included)
       came back.
    3. Called on the same ``inputs`` and ``kwargs``, both operators
       return the same output. Comparison is exact: arrays (anything
       exposing ``__array__``) must match in type, shape, dtype and
       bytes, so ``NaN`` equals ``NaN`` but ``-0.0`` differs from
       ``0.0``; floats compare exactly (``NaN`` equal to ``NaN``);
       dicts (whatever their key order, as with ``==``), lists and
       tuples are compared item by item; any other value with ``==``.
       Array outputs need NumPy installed.

    Both operators receive the same input objects: an operator that
    mutates its input breaks the carrier contract and may fail here.

    Args:
        op: The operator (or `Sequential` / `Graph`) under test.
        *inputs: Positional inputs for the call.
        **kwargs: Keyword inputs for the call (a `Graph`'s named inputs).

    Returns:
        The rebuilt operator, for further checks.

    Raises:
        RuntimeError: if ``op``, or any operator nested in it, is marked
            ``forbid_in_yaml`` (its config is a debug payload, so the
            round trip is not expected to hold).
        AssertionError: on the first violated property, naming the
            operator.

    Example::

        >>> from pipekit import Const
        >>> from pipekit.testing import assert_round_trip
        >>> back = assert_round_trip(Const(3), "ignored")
        >>> back.value
        3
    """
    name = type(op).__name__
    flagged = check_pickleable(op)
    if flagged:
        names = ", ".join(type(f).__name__ for f in flagged)
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"assert_round_trip({name}): refuses operators marked forbid_in_yaml "
            f"({names}); their config is a debug payload, not a round trip."
        )

    try:
        back = loads(dumps(op))
    except Exception as exc:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{name}: loads(dumps(op)) failed with {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        ) from exc
    _require(
        type(back) is type(op),
        f"{name}: loads(dumps(op)) rebuilt a {type(back).__name__}",
    )

    expected_hash = pipeline_hash(op)
    actual_hash = pipeline_hash(back)
    _require(
        actual_hash == expected_hash,
        (
            f"{name}: pipeline_hash changed across loads(dumps(op)) "
            f"({expected_hash[:12]} -> {actual_hash[:12]}).\n"
            f"  before: {op.state!r}\n  after:  {back.state!r}"
        ),
    )

    expected = op(*inputs, **kwargs)
    try:
        actual = back(*inputs, **kwargs)
    except Exception as exc:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{name}: the rebuilt operator raised {type(exc).__name__} on inputs "
            f"the original accepts: {exc}"
        ) from exc
    _assert_same(actual, expected, f"{name} output")
    return back

def public_operators(module: ModuleType) -> dict[str, type[Operator]]:
    """Every `Operator` subclass named in ``module.__all__``.

    Args:
        module: An imported package or module with an ``__all__``.

    Returns:
        ``{public name: class}``, in ``__all__`` order. Abstract bases
        (`Operator` itself, `StatefulOperator`, …) are included: the
        caller decides what to skip.

    Raises:
        AttributeError: if ``module`` has no ``__all__``.
    """
    found: dict[str, type[Operator]] = {}
    for name in module.__all__:
        obj = getattr(module, name)
        if isinstance(obj, type) and issubclass(obj, Operator):
            found[name] = obj
    return found

docs.title: Background — from toolz to pipekit
docs.text:
Where pipekit comes from, and why its operators are classes.

pipekit is toolz with each function replaced by a typed class. This page shows what that inheritance gives, the six things plain functions cannot carry, and why operators settled on a concrete base class while the data flowing through them did not. It is background: for what ships and when to reach for it, read the tour of the core.

About this page Reading time about 15 minutes Audience anyone who wants to know why pipekit is shaped the way it is Companions Tour of the core (what ships), Patterns (where it is used), Concepts (the mental model in ten minutes) Checked against toolz 1.1 and pipekit 0.0.2; every output below is from a real run History First written as Report 1 of the GeoStack design reports, which now point here

docs.title: Why this page exists
docs.text: The pipekit design makes more sense once you have seen three things: what it inherited from toolz, what that inheritance cannot do, and why moving from "any function" to a typed operator class is the right call rather than over-engineering. This is the motivation layer; the operators themselves are in the tour of the core.

docs.title: toolz as the ancestor
docs.text: pytoolz/toolz is pipekit's explicit intellectual ancestor. Looking at it directly is the fastest way to see which idea pipekit carries forward and what it adds. Its functional core is a dozen primitives.

docs.title: The toolz.functoolz surface
docs.text:
The functoolz primitives pipekit inherits from.

toolz primitive What it does identity(x) pass the value through unchanged pipe(value, *funcs) apply functions left to right to a value compose(*funcs) right-to-left composition: f(g(h(x))) compose_left(*funcs) left-to-right composition juxt(*funcs) several outputs: juxt(f, g)(x) is (f(x), g(x)) do(f, x) run f(x) for its side effect and return x complement(pred) negate a predicate excepts(exceptions, func, handler) catch the listed exceptions while applying func memoize(func) cache results by input curry partial application, as a class wrapper thread_first, thread_last Clojure-style threading macros flip(f, a, b) call f(b, a)

toolz also ships itertoolz (about 30 functions on iterables) and dicttoolz (about 15 on dicts). pipekit only really inherits from functoolz.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
toolz says a pipeline is a sequence of pure functions, composed with pipe or compose. Each function is responsible for its transform and nothing else; metadata, types and side effects are someone else's problem.

A toolz pipeline. do must come from toolz.curried to be used without its value.
from toolz import pipe
from toolz.curried import do

pipe(
    "  HELLO  ",
    str.strip,
    str.lower,
    do(print),                  # side effect: prints "hello"
    lambda s: s.split("l"),
)
# → ['he', '', 'o']

This is functional composition over plain Python. Functions are values, composition is an operation, and side effects are explicit (do). It is elegant and minimal, and it directly inspired pipekit's | syntax, the Sequential shape, the Tap / Sink split, and the juxt / Fanout pair.

docs.title: One-to-one mappings to pipekit
docs.text:
Almost every pipekit primitive has a toolz ancestor. The mapping is tight enough that the most accurate one-line description of pipekit is toolz, with each function replaced by a typed class.

toolz primitives and their pipekit counterparts.

toolz pipekit What pipekit's version adds pipe(value, *funcs) pipe(value, *operators), Sequential(operators)(value) operators carry config; a readable repr; reuse compose_left(*funcs) compose_left(...), op1 \| op2 \| op3 \| flattens into one Sequential; class-typed steps compose(*funcs) compose(...) the same, in mathematical order do(f, x) Tap(fn), Sink(write_fn) the closure is owned by an operator with a name; marked forbid_in_yaml juxt(f, g, h) juxt(...) (tuple) and Fanout({...}) (dict) both shapes; named outputs for downstream steps memoize Cache, with Memoize as an alias config-aware hashing excepts Try, Coalesce operator-shaped arms; an explicit exception list complement complement ships as a plain function identity Identity an operator, so it composes everywhere curry implicit in __init__ an operator's constructor is its partial application

The same pipeline in both libraries shows the difference. Both outputs below are from real runs.

toolzpipekit A toolz composition prints its steps as raw function objects, in reverse order.
from toolz import compose_left

steps = compose_left(str.strip, str.lower, lambda s: s.split("l"))
print(steps)
# Compose(<function <lambda> at 0x7f…>, <method 'lower' of 'str' objects>,
#         <method 'strip' of 'str' objects>)
The same steps as pipekit operators: named, indexable, in order.
from pipekit import Lambda, Tap

steps = (
    Lambda(str.strip) | Lambda(str.lower) | Tap(print)
    | Lambda(lambda s: s.split("l"))
)
print(steps)
# Sequential([Lambda(name='strip'), Lambda(name='lower'),
#             Tap(name='print'), Lambda(name='<lambda>')])
steps[2]                   # → Tap(name='print')
steps("  HELLO  ")         # prints "hello"; → ['he', '', 'o']

toolz is the design template. pipekit is the typed, introspectable, serialisable variant of the same idea.

docs.title: Where toolz stops being enough
docs.text:
toolz handles the mechanics of function composition cleanly. Six things are beyond it, and each is why the domain libraries needed more.

The six gaps, and where pipekit puts each one.

Gap What toolz gives Where it lives in pipekit Status Introspection a repr of raw function objects named operators, Sequential.__getitem__, summary() ships Serialisation nothing get_config, dumps / loads, from_state flat operators only Dual-mode dispatch eager calls only Operator.__call__ switches on Node inputs ships Control flow Python if / match outside the pipeline Branch, Switch, Try, Coalesce ships Shape tracking Any → Any Signature, Sequential.summary() ships; needs signatures Closure discipline any closure, silently the forbid_in_yaml class flag ships

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text: A toolz composition is not opaque: Compose prints its steps (the toolz tab above). But it prints them as raw function objects, in reverse order, with lambdas anonymous and no configuration or per-step state to inspect. That is fine at an interactive prompt. For a 14-step preprocessing pipeline that has to be audited, you want named steps, in order, that you can index (steps[2]) and summarise.

docs.title: Serialisation
docs.text:
toolz pipelines are tuples of function references and closures. They do not round-trip to YAML, JSON or a Hydra config, and they cannot be shipped to a worker process and rebuilt. Every deployment shape in the patterns (an ETL job, a web service, a tile server, a regulatory artifact, an orchestrator) needs serialisation in some form.

pipekit gives every operator a get_config(), and a pipeline's state is its whole configuration: each nested operator as its own record, and for a Graph every node and its wiring. That record round-trips through JSON, and through _target_ YAML with pipekit-experiment's HydraConfigLoader:

A nested pipeline round-trips, from a real run.
import pipekit as pk
from pipekit import Cache, Const, Identity, Sequential

pipe = Cache(Sequential([Const(3), Identity()]))
back = pk.loads(pk.dumps(pipe))
back.state == pipe.state                         # → True
pk.pipeline_hash(back) == pk.pipeline_hash(pipe)  # → True

Only operators that hold a closure (Lambda, Tap, a Branch predicate) stay out: they are flagged forbid_in_yaml, and loads refuses them wherever they sit in the tree.

docs.title: Dual-mode dispatch
docs.text: toolz functions only run eagerly. You cannot pass a symbolic placeholder through them to build a graph that runs later. Graph building (the Input / Node API) needs the same callable to behave differently depending on whether its argument is data or a placeholder. In pipekit that switch lives once, in Operator.__call__: any Node argument builds a graph node, and anything else calls _apply.

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text: In a toolz-style pipeline, a conditional is a Python if or match outside the pipeline, which splits the pipeline apart wherever one is needed. pipekit makes conditionals first-class operators (Branch, Switch, Try, Coalesce), composable inside a Sequential like any other step.

docs.title: Shape tracking
docs.text: Every toolz step is Any → Any. For scientific data that hides structure worth surfacing: named dimensions, units, a coordinate system. pipekit's Signature lets an operator declare what it accepts and returns, and Sequential.summary() prints a Keras-style table that catches a shape mismatch when the pipeline is built, not deep in a hot loop. Operators that declare no signature show ? in that table, so the payoff grows as more operators declare one.

docs.title: Closure discipline
docs.text:
toolz accepts any closure. That is right for interactive work and wrong for pipelines that must be audited: a closure cannot be inspected for what it captures, serialised, or rebuilt on a worker. pipekit's answer is a class flag. Operators whose constructor takes a closure declare forbid_in_yaml = True (Tap, Lambda, Sink, Branch, Switch, Coalesce, ShapeTrace, Quarantine, AssertCallable), and a loader can refuse them. Operators that only nest other operators, such as Try, Retry or Cache, are not flagged: a walker finds the flagged children inside them.

The gaps in one line

pipekit is what toolz becomes when the pipeline is a first-class object: printable, configurable, summarisable, dispatchable, and bound by rules about what it may contain.

docs.title: The trajectory: functions, Protocols, typed entities
docs.text:
The question is how pipekit moved from raw functions, through Protocols, to typed entities. The answer differs for the steps of a pipeline (operators) and for the data flowing through it (carriers), so the two are told separately.

Operators settled on a typed class; carriers use all three stages at once.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
1 · Functions2 · Protocols3 · Typed base class

The toolz shape: an operator is a Python function. Maximum flexibility, zero boilerplate.

def my_op(x):
    return ...

pipe(value, my_op, other_op, third_op)

Buys you: any existing function adapts trivially, with no subclassing and no dependency beyond toolz.

Costs you: no config, no readable repr, no serialisation, no dispatch, no flags, no state, and no reuse beyond reusing the function.

The natural next thought is to write a Protocol for what an operator looks like. Anything structurally compatible counts; nothing has to inherit.

from typing import Protocol

class OperatorLike(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, x): ...
    def get_config(self) -> dict: ...

Buys you: structural typing. Tools can recognise operator-shaped objects without forcing inheritance, which suits third-party code that does not import your library.

Costs you: a Protocol is a check, not a base class.

  • No default implementations. Every implementer rebuilds get_config, __repr__ and __or__; there is no super() to reuse.
  • No class-level flags. forbid_in_yaml and _terminal describe an operator's contract, not its instances, and a Protocol cannot carry them cleanly.
  • No shared mechanism. Dual-mode dispatch is infrastructure every operator needs; with a Protocol each one reimplements it.
  • No class registry. Operator.from_state rebuilds an operator by walking cls.__subclasses__(); a Protocol has no subclasses to walk.

Verdict: a Protocol is the right tool to check that something is operator-shaped, and the wrong tool to be the operator base. (pipekit still uses Protocols where they fit: for the seams algorithm libraries plug into without importing it; see Protocols.)

Where pipekit landed. A simplified view of pipekit/_base/operator.py:

The Operator base class, simplified.
class Operator(ConfigMixin):
    forbid_in_yaml: ClassVar[bool] = False   # closure-holding operators set True
    _terminal: ClassVar[bool] = False        # may only end a Sequential

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):     # dual-mode dispatch
        if any(isinstance(a, Node) for a in args):
            ...                              # build a graph node
        return self._apply(*args, **kwargs)  # run eagerly

    def _apply(self, *args, **kwargs):       # the one method subclasses write
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __or__(self, other) -> Sequential:   # pipe syntax, defined once
        ...

    @classmethod
    def from_state(cls, state) -> Operator:  # walks cls.__subclasses__()
        ...

Buys you:

  • __init__ carries config, get_config() (derived by ConfigMixin) exposes it, and from_state rebuilds from it.
  • __or__ is defined once, so every subclass gets pipe syntax for free.
  • Dual-mode __call__ is defined once; subclasses only write _apply.
  • Class flags (forbid_in_yaml, _terminal) are visible to Sequential's validation and to any loader.
  • IDEs and type checkers see the whole surface.

Costs you:

  • Subclassing is more ceremony than a function (class NDVI(Operator)).
  • A third-party function does not adapt for free; Lambda is the escape hatch, and ConfigMixin keeps the boilerplate small.
  • More framework code to maintain.

Verdict: the right design for operators. Every responsibility has a natural home, and the cost is a one-time decision to subclass. geotoolz and xrtoolz each arrived here independently before the base class moved into pipekit, which is the strongest sign it is right.

docs.title: Carriers
docs.text:
The carrier trajectory is different, and not settled.

1 · Any2 · Protocols3 · Concrete types

pipekit's core uses Carrier = Any. The framework does not care what flows through; operators that need structure check it in their own signatures.

Buys you: maximum flexibility. Composition works the same whether the carrier is a NumPy array, an xr.DataArray, a DataFrame, an AnnData, a scalar or a user type, and test pipelines can run on scalars.

Costs you: operators that do want structure (named axes, coordinate systems, units) duck-check it every time, and there is no shared metadata surface.

The ecosystem has converged on Protocol-shaped array descriptions through the Array API standard: numpy.ndarray, jax.Array, cupy.ndarray, torch.Tensor and dask.array.Array all expose __array_namespace__. Operators written against it declare the Protocol and work across backends; pipekit-array is where they live.

Buys you: an operator written once runs on NumPy, JAX, CuPy and PyTorch arrays, which is real value for cross-framework pipelines.

Costs you: the Array API becomes a dependency; operators call the namespace (xp.mean(x)) rather than NumPy (np.mean(x)); and some operations do not generalise cleanly, NaN handling for one.

Domain libraries type their operators to a specific carrier. In the GeoStack, geotoolz uses GeoTensor and xrtoolz uses xr.DataArray or xr.Dataset.

Buys you: rich metadata used natively. geotoolz operators read .crs and .transform without defensive checks; xrtoolz operators use .dims and .coords directly.

Costs you: each library is locked to its carrier, so Sequential([geotoolz_op, xrtoolz_op]) does not compose across them, and a carrier-specific operator is written once per library.

docs.title: Where pipekit lands
docs.text:
The two trajectories, resolved separately.

Axis Where it lands Status Operators a typed concrete base class, pipekit.Operator settled Carriers, pipekit core Carrier = Any settled: the core stays carrier-agnostic Carriers, multi-backend Array API Protocols, in pipekit-array in progress Carriers, domain libraries your own: GeoTensor in geotoolz, xr.DataArray / xr.Dataset in xrtoolz, … in use

It was never one arc from functions to Protocols to typed entities. It was two trajectories that shared vocabulary. Operators started at toolz functions, considered Protocols, and landed on a typed base class. Carriers are still at all three stages at once, by design: each library uses the stage that serves it. Telling them as one story blurs the picture.

docs.title: Why typed operators are not over-engineering
docs.text:
"Just use functions" is tempting: less code, faster to write, familiar to anyone who has used toolz, no subclassing.

The case for typed operators is that the six gaps above have no function-shaped solutions. Each needs somewhere to live: get_config on the operator, forbid_in_yaml on the class, dispatch in __call__, subclass walking in from_state. A function is the wrong host for all of them.

So the argument is not that classes beat functions. It is that the responsibilities pipekit takes on are class-shaped. Remove them (no introspection, no serialisation, no dispatch, no flags) and you are left with toolz, which is a perfectly good answer for problems that fit it. pipekit's problems do not.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• The tour of the core turns this background into what ships: the toolz-style functions, the Operator base with the machinery for the six gaps, composition, control flow, observers, caching, QC, shape inference, parallelism, serialisation and state.
  • Patterns maps it onto the shapes real deployments take, each linked to a worked tutorial.
  • The sister libraries that narrow the carrier (pipekit-array, geotoolz, xrtoolz) and the wider stack are in the GeoStack design reports.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The design synthesises two upstream sources:

  • The master plan: research_journal_v2/notes/geotoolz/master_plan/toolz_9_pipekit_train.md (Report 11). Vision, three training shapes, package scope, reproducibility story.
  • The eqx_trainer design doc in jej_vc_snippets/design_docs/eqx_trainer/. Concrete JAX-native stack (Equinox + Optax + Grain + Orbax) that becomes the v0.1 reference adapter inside pipekit_train.adapters.equinox.

Where the two diverge, this doc resolves the tension explicitly — see decisions.md for the ADRs.

docs.title: 1. Where pipekit-train sits in the stack
